72843720B863019116732.name: Centro
72843720B863019116732.summary:
Centro contains two of Italy's six highest-victim regions for anti-LGBT violence (Lazio, Toscana per the Progetto Gionata 2012–2025 region-by-region study) and saw an activist assaulted at the Piceno Pride march in Ascoli Piceno (June 2025) with his flag seized and destroyed. Rome Pride was also targeted politically. However, the unit also contains the strongest positive institutional response found anywhere in Italy: a January 2025 Bologna first-instance conviction that recognised a "transphobic motive" behind a punitive rape of a trans sex worker, awarded damages, and — for the first time — admitted the Movimento Identità Trans as civil party. This is a judicial signal that transphobic violence is prosecuted as a distinct aggravating factor, and it applies to visitors who would rely on the same courts.

Net deviation: +0.02 above the national score (0.50). The high-victim data for Lazio and Toscana are concerning but are offset by the Bologna precedent and the absence of any criminalisation, facility ban, or enforcement mechanism targeting a visitor. The Ascoli Piceno incident is a single event with no patterned institutional failure. Compared to Nord-Ovest (0.47), Centro trades lower violence-concentration (no Milano/Torino killing or Brianza Roman-salute episode) for a stronger judicial response; compared to Sud (0.44), Centro lacks the railway-station public-exposure incidents and the ILGA-Europe "geographic spread" finding.
72843720B863019116732.modelContext: Rome/Florence/Bologna: the institutional heart — Rome's scene is large if more discreet than Milan, Bologna historically Italy's most LGBT-friendly city (Arcigay birthplace, leftist municipal tradition), Tuscany tourism envelope; central regions combine visibility with the strongest civil-society infrastructure.

72843720B99597932318450.name: Nord-Ovest
72843720B99597932318450.summary:
Nord-Ovest bundles Italy's two most protective municipal measures for transgender people with two of the six highest-victim regions in the Progetto Gionata dataset. Milano operates Italy's first "registro di genere" (chosen name on civic documents, transport subscriptions, staff badges) and Torino runs "Identità Alias" at the comune and public libraries — practical tools that determine whether a gender-nonconforming visitor is humiliated at a ticket window or not. Against this, Lombardy and Piedmont are named as high-violence regions; a 28-year-old trans woman was found dead in Alessandria (Oct 2025), linked to a robbery series targeting vulnerable people, and right-wing militants gave Roman salutes along the Brianza Pride route (Sept 2025).

The institutional responses are notably good: the Carabinieri scientific section produced prompt charges with wiretaps and confessions in the Alessandria killing; the Digos moved pre-emptively at Brianza Pride and "struck out at birth" the spark. Lombardy's 2015 "natural family" motion and rejection of WHO sex-ed standards are dated climate signals with no visitor-facing enforcement mechanism.

Net deviation: −0.03 from the national score (0.50). The violence concentration is real for a traveler, but the protective registries and the quality of institutional responses partially offset it. Compared to Centro (0.52), Nord-Ovest lacks a landmark transphobic-motive conviction but has more practical visitor-facing protections and more documented violence. Compared to Nord-Est (0.47), the protective measures here are concrete and used, not merely symbolic motions.
72843720B99597932318450.modelContext: Milan/Turin/Genoa: Italy's wealthiest, most cosmopolitan northwest — Milan has the country's deepest scene and most efficient institutions; Ligurian coast tourism; regional politics mixed but northern society is the most European-facing.

72843720B59566147937015.name: Nord-Est
72843720B59566147937015.summary:
Nord-Est's distinguishing evidence is Veneto's institutionalised hostility: the regional council approved motion 340 backing "those who fight in defence of the natural family," created an official "Festa della Famiglia Naturale" on the school calendar, and formally rejected the WHO Regional Office's Standards for Sexuality Education in Europe — all published in the region's official bulletin (BUR). A 2014 motion preceded this. A gay student in Venezia was stalked by three self-identified fascists in 2025, but this is a single incident with no patterned institutional failure. No violence data names Veneto, Trentino-Alto Adige, or Friuli-Venezia Giulia among the six highest-victim regions.

The natural-family motions and WHO rejection are official acts of hostility and a clear climate signal to a visitor, but they do not criminalise, fine, or create enforcement exposure for a transgender person crossing the Brenner or landing in Venice. No special-statute region used its expanded legislative competence on gender matters. The practical visitor risk from the policy layer is limited to being unwelcome, not arrested.

Net deviation: −0.03 from the national score (0.50), reflecting the official posture. Compared to Nord-Ovest (0.47), the score is similar but for opposite reasons: Nord-Est lacks both the high-victim data and the protective registries that characterise its western neighbour. Compared to Centro (0.52), the absence of a positive institutional response like Bologna's transphobic-motive conviction means the official hostility is unmitigated.
72843720B59566147937015.modelContext: Venice/Verona/Bologna-adjacent northeast: wealthy, Catholic-league traditionalism in Veneto (documented regional-council hostility), but strong municipal institutions; Trento/Bolzano autonomous provinces are Alpine-central-European in culture.

72843720B88210905209841.name: Sud
72843720B88210905209841.summary:
Sud contains Campania and Puglia, two of the six highest-victim regions in the Progetto Gionata 2012–2025 dataset, and multiple documented public-space incidents directly relevant to a traveler: a homophobic assault in Scampia, Naples (March 2025), part of ILGA-Europe's finding of a "troubling increase in the geographic spread" of bias violence; and a verbal attack culminating in threats of stabbing against an Arcigay activist at the EAV railway station in Torre Annunziata (October 2025) — a public transit setting any visitor could encounter. A kidnapping, violence, and robbery occurred in Reggio Calabria (May 2024), though the squadra mobile's swift intervention drew public commendation from Arcigay.

Puglia's Taranto and Basilicata's Termoli hosted Onda Pride marches in 2025, indicating continued public LGBTQ presence. No special-statute region in the Sud used expanded competence against transgender people. No criminal facility bans or enforcement mechanisms target visitors. The violence is criminal and street-level, not state-imposed, but its concentration and public-transit exposure raise the probability of encounter for a traveler.

Net deviation: −0.06 from the national score (0.50). Two high-victim regions plus railway-station and street incidents pattern above the national average. Compared to Centro (0.52), Sud lacks a landmark positive judicial response and carries more public-space exposure. Compared to Isole (0.45), the scores are close; Sud edges lower on the quantitative victim data (two of six top regions) while Isole carries the heavier qualitative pattern (suicides, sustained rising bullying).
72843720B88210905209841.modelContext: Naples/Bari/Palermo-adjacent mainland south: Campania and Puglia carry Italy's highest documented anti-LGBT violence rates AND strong femminiello/traditional gender-variant cultures in Naples — the south is simultaneously the most dangerous and the most culturally gender-fluid part of Italy; institutional protection weakest, family honor culture strongest.

72843720B81376294924159.name: Isole
72843720B81376294924159.summary:
Isole's evidence is dominated by Sicily. In April 2025, three young men were beaten in a Catania fast-food restaurant at roughly 5 a.m. solely because they were gay; victims were hospitalised and the prosecutor's office reconstructed the assault sequence from video that circulated publicly. A mother was attacked in Catania (July 2025) in an incident Arcigay named in a national statement accusing the government of "exposing us to violence." A June 2026 survey of Sicilian reporting describes a sustained pattern of rising homophobic bullying, violence against the LGBTQIA+ community, and associated suicides, listing multiple cases — this is a patterned finding, not a single incident. Favignana (Trapani) hosted an Onda Pride march, showing visibility persists alongside the harm. No Sardinia-specific evidence was found.

Sicily is not among the six highest-victim regions in the quantitative Gionata data, but the 2026 qualitative pattern (multiple cases, suicides) and the Catania hospitalisation assault indicate a severity profile that elevates real risk for a visitor in nightlife and public-street settings. No special-statute region (Sicilia, Sardegna) used expanded legislative competence against transgender people. The violence is criminal, not state-enforced.

Net deviation: −0.05 from the national score (0.50). The sustained Sicilian pattern with suicides and the hospitalisation-level assault in a tourist-accessible city push this below national. Compared to Sud (0.44), Isole is marginally higher because it lacks two-of-six top-victim-region data and the public-transit stabbing-threat exposure, but the qualitative severity (suicides, hospitalisation) is comparable. Compared to Centro (0.52), the absence of a positive institutional response like Bologna's transphobic-motive conviction leaves the violence unmitigated.
72843720B81376294924159.modelContext: Sicily and Sardinia: Catania beating (2025) documented Sicilian risk; Sicily has historic femminiello-adjacent traditions; Sardinia is insular-traditional with low immigration and strong family codes; both islands have small organized scenes in Palermo/Cagliari and tourism envelopes in Taormina (historic gay-tourism destination since the 19th century) and Costa Smeralda.

82249235B5553315981608.name: Alberta
82249235B5553315981608.summary:
Alberta is the only Canadian jurisdiction to pass laws targeting transgender people as a class and then shield those laws from judicial review. The Education Amendment Act 2024 (Bill 27) mandates parental notification/consent before staff use a student's gender-related preferred name or pronouns (in force 1 Sep 2025); the Health Statutes Amendment Act 2024 (Bill 26) prohibits puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors; and a vital-statistics rule was amended. Bill 9 (2025) invoked Charter s.33 over all three laws, and after it passed the Court of King's Bench lifted the injunction that had paused the care ban — a government appeal succeeded, removing the injunction.

These school and healthcare provisions are primarily resident-facing and carry small traveler-facing weight. The more directly relevant signal is the documented street-level pattern in Calgary: pastor Derek Reimer led repeated disruptions of library drag-storytime events from 2023, shouting slurs at parents and children; events were cancelled or postponed as threats escalated. His conviction for harassing a librarian was upheld on appeal, and acquittals on disturbance/mischief were overturned with a new trial ordered; a further breach conviction followed in 2026. The institutional response is mixed-leaning-positive, but the pattern of cancelled public expression events and the government's willingness to override courts constitute a clear escalation in provincial posture.

Deviation: 0.10 below the national score of 0.86. The notwithstanding clause — described by legal commentators as "the nuclear option" — signals a government that legislates against trans people and defeats judicial review; combined with the Calgary disruption pattern (traveler-facing cancellation of public events), this places Alberta well below any other Canadian province. The 2021 gender-related homicide rate (0.68/100k, second-highest provincial) is a weak proxy only and not trans-specific.

Compared to Saskatchewan (0.79), Alberta is materially lower: both used s.33 to immunise trans-targeting legislation, but Alberta adds a multi-year, event-level pattern of public disruption at libraries that a visitor could encounter directly. Compared to the national score, the gap reflects that no other province has paired legislative targeting with a judicial-override shield and a documented cancellation pattern in one unit.
82249235B5553315981608.modelContext: Calgary/Edmonton scenes exist but Alberta is the conservative-prairie exception: strongest religious-right political current in Canada, though Canadian law still binds — climate difference, not legal difference.

82249235B71336988791422.name: Saskatchewan
82249235B71336988791422.summary:
Saskatchewan's provincial government enacted a parental-consent rule for students under 16 (name/pronoun policy, Aug 2023), which the Court of King's Bench struck down in UR Pride Centre for Sexuality and Gender Diversity v Saskatchewan, 2023 SKKB 204. The government responded by legislating the rule into the Education Act (s.197.4, The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023) and invoking Charter s.33 to immunise it from judicial review. The matter returned to the Court of Appeal as Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74 (Aug 2025).

The school policy is resident-facing and carries small traveler-facing weight. The significant signal is the government's pattern of overriding a court that found the law unconstitutional — a structural escalation in provincial posture toward trans people that a visitor would register as hostile climate (provincial statements, board-meeting activity, protest presence). No documented street-level disruption or cancellation of public events was found in the dossier. The 2021 gender-related homicide rate (1.03 per 100k, highest provincial) is a weak, non-trans-specific proxy.

Deviation: 0.07 below the national score of 0.86. The notwithstanding clause use places Saskatchewan clearly below provinces without legislative hostility, but the absence of a documented traveler-facing incident series (unlike Alberta's Calgary pattern) limits the gap. Compared to Alberta (0.76), Saskatchewan scores higher because the legislative weapon is identical but the street-level cancellation pattern is absent. Compared to British Columbia (0.82), Saskatchewan is lower because BC had disruptions but no provincial override of courts.
82249235B71336988791422.modelContext: Rural prairie conservatism; small scenes in Saskatoon/Regina; institutions function.

82249235B4167839012994.name: New Brunswick
82249235B4167839012994.summary:
New Brunswick is the clearest Canadian case of a provincial government reversing course on trans rights within one election cycle. Policy 713 (2020) originally protected 2SLGBTQIA+ student privacy and inclusion. In July 2023, the Higgs government amended it to require parental consent for under-16 name/pronoun use, triggering protests outside the legislature. The Holt government reversed the amendment on 19 December 2024, effective 1 January 2025: parental consent is now "encouraged but no longer required" for students of any age, with a "presumed capacity" concept based on child-and-youth-advocate recommendations. The revised policy text extends its language to "people visiting schools" (student teachers, visiting professionals), so current rules technically reach non-residents presenting in classrooms.

Deviation: 0.02 below the national score of 0.86. The reversal is a strong positive institutional response — a government that legislated against trans students repealed the provision after one term. The residual signal is the demonstrated capacity for hostile policy within an election cycle and the 2023 protest period, which create a slightly higher baseline of political volatility than provinces that never legislated against trans people. No street-level disruption of public expression events was documented.

Compared to Alberta (0.76) and Saskatchewan (0.79), New Brunswick is materially higher: it did not use the notwithstanding clause, and its hostile policy was reversed rather than immunised from judicial review. Compared to the national score, the gap is small and time-sensitive — the current effective policy is protective, and further reversal would bring New Brunswick to or above the national level.
82249235B4167839012994.modelContext: Bilingual Atlantic province; socially traditional; small Moncton/Fredericton scene.

14339913B23556801435424.name: Scotland
14339913B23556801435424.summary:
Scotland diverges from the UK baseline in one live, visitor-relevant direction: the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021 (in force 1 April 2024) created the UK's only dedicated transgender-identity hate-crime aggravation. COPFS reported 104 charges carrying that aggravation in 2025-26 (up 21%), and Police Scotland recorded 8,538 hate crimes in 2024-25 — anti-trans offending in Scotland is named, counted and charged as a distinct category, while in England and Wales it is statistically invisible in official recording. For an assaulted or harassed visitor that is the difference between a crime the system is built to recognise and one it is not. The wider climate corroborates the law: Holyrood passed expansive gender-recognition reform by a two-thirds majority, and Scottish public opinion on LGBT equality runs consistently ahead of the UK average (British Social Attitudes).

What does not count against Scotland as local hostility: the Section 35 veto of that reform and the June 2026 Court of Session ruling voiding the Scottish Prison Service's trans custody guidance were both applications of UK-wide law and the UK Supreme Court's biological-sex definition — the same mechanisms visitors face in every British nation, already priced into the national score (0.48). They erased Scotland's attempt to rise above that baseline; they did not push it below. Scotland therefore scores above the national anchor: the strand machinery plus the most trans-accepting electorate and government in the Isles. Vs Wales (≈0.51): inclusive posture, no charging strand. Vs England: no strand and recording invisibility; vs Northern Ireland (0.42): withdrawn school guidance, stalled hate-crime inclusion.
14339913B23556801435424.modelContext: Edinburgh/Glasgow scenes; Scottish law and politics consistently more progressive on LGBT rights than Westminster; strong institutions.

31927357B79016588373767.name: Distrito Federal
31927357B79016588373767.summary:
CDMX recorded the highest transfeminicide toll in the country in 2024 — 17 LGBT+ homicides, of which 11 were trans women — and remains among the highest-count states in 2025. The raw violence data is a negative signal for a visitor, though part of the elevated count reflects the city's superior reporting infrastructure rather than proportionally higher danger.

Counterbalanced by the strongest institutional response of any Mexican state: transfeminicide made a distinct crime in July 2024 (Ley Paola Buenrostro); a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit created December 2024 with mandatory 72h/48h action protocols (Acuerdo FGJCDMX/04/2025); a new Gender Police with 30 patrol units launched August 2025. Long-standing LGR since 2014, extended to 12-year-olds by 2021 decree. For a visitor assaulted in CDMX, there is trained machinery to investigate; in Nuevo León (0.40) or Michoacán (0.40) there is none.

Modestly above the national 0.55: the protective and investigative framework is the strongest in Mexico and materially changes what a visitor who encounters violence or discrimination faces after the fact, even though the pre-violence risk data is the country's worst.
31927357B79016588373767.modelContext: Mexico City: North America's most established LGBT scene after US/Canadian metros; Pride draws hundreds of thousands; city human-rights institutions functional; full anonymity in Roma/Zona Rosa.

31927357B30741484985331.name: Nuevo Leon
31927357B30741484985331.summary:
Three trans women murdered in less than a week in July 2024; five transfeminicides recorded for the year (second only to CDMX). Activists reported six killed in a short period and accused three levels of government of rights omissions. Nuevo León's penal code contains no transfeminicide offence, and its 2019 hate-crime provision covers sexual orientation but not gender identity — meaning a visitor assaulted in Monterrey faces a legal framework with no specific protective category.

Legislative response has been refusal: an initiative filed by Colectivo Casa Trans was 'ignored and finally lapsed,' prompting a 50+-day protest encampment outside the state congress still ongoing in January 2026. A PT deputy in 2026 could only ask the congress to 'unfreeze' the bill. There is no investigative unit, no protocol, and no named offence to invoke.

Well below the national 0.55 (−0.15). Versus CDMX (0.57), which pairs similar lethality with a dedicated investigation unit, mandatory-response protocols, and a gender police force, Nuevo León's absence of any transfeminicide offence or investigative machinery is the decisive divergence. Versus Nayarit (0.57), which was first in the country to typify the crime in 2024, Nuevo León's explicit legislative refusal is the opposite signal.
31927357B30741484985331.modelContext: Monterrey: wealthy industrial north; state-level 'morality' legal actions documented; conservative business-Catholic culture; cartel presence.

31927357B49073316106075.name: Michoacan de Ocampo
31927357B49073316106075.summary:
The state has not typified hate crime at all, per its own LGBT+ welfare sub-director (June 2026). Six LGBT homicides recorded in the first four and a half months of 2026 alone, including 'Daniela,' a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia (suspect arrested — a positive institutional response). Two additional deaths in Morelia in April 2026 were linked by the attorney general to organised crime. The state's own official locates most attacks in Tierra Caliente, a comarca under armed-group influence, while a civil-society count attributes 102 killings of gay men to named municipalities between 2015–2024.

Activists report victims are no longer attended to and the violence is not acknowledged by the state. The arrest in the Daniela case is a single positive data point against a backdrop of collective non-acknowledgment. No transfeminicide offence, no hate-crime typification, no investigative protocol.

Well below the national 0.55 (−0.15). Versus Veracruz (0.42), which at least has a gender-identity civil-code reform (2025), Michoacán lacks even that; its armed-group amplifier in Tierra Caliente and border-with-Jalisco escalation make the violence pattern harder to escape. Versus CDMX (0.57), where a dedicated unit and mandatory-response protocol exist, Michoacán has no legal machinery whatsoever.
31927357B49073316106075.modelContext: Cartel (CJNG/Familia legacy) contested; conservative Catholic heartland (Morelia/Uruguay valley tradition).

31927357B5337219705256.name: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
31927357B5337219705256.summary:
Veracruz led the national LGBT+ fatality count for four consecutive years (2021: 10 recorded violent deaths). In 2025, at least 15 hate crimes were recorded; a running total of 460 unresolved hate-crime cases was reported in January 2025. Activists cite 'rezago y archivamiento de expedientes' (deliberate filing and archiving of cases); the state prosecutor's office has lost investigative files entirely. Emblematic cases have arrests but no final sentences. The 2025 murder of 'Luis M' in an Oluta motel continued the pattern, with the state observatory counting 9 hate crimes earlier that same year.

The only institutional counterweight is recent: Veracruz passed its gender-identity civil-code reform in 2025 (no age limit), the second-to-last of the 22 legislating states. Before that, a visitor or resident had no legal route to correct documents. The absence of any functioning investigation or prosecution machinery — distinct from other states where laws exist but enforcement is weak — makes the impunity here total.

Well below the national 0.55 (−0.13). Versus Guanajuato (0.53), which also carries sustained violence but has a comprehensive diversity law and court-forced recognition procedure, Veracruz's four-year lethality record combined with explicit case-archiving and lost files represents the worst enforcement climate. Versus Nayarit (0.57), which typified the offence first in the country, Veracruz's legal framework arrived latest and is least functional.
31927357B5337219705256.modelContext: High violent-crime rates; conservative Gulf-coast society; weak institutions.

31927357B6525686063804.name: Oaxaca
31927357B6525686063804.summary:
In May 2024, the organising brotherhood of the Vela San Vicente Ferrer 'Goola' in Juchitán circulated a written invitation stating 'men dressed as women will not be admitted.' Muxe activists including poet-lawyer Elvis Guerra filed a CONAPRED discrimination complaint, saying 'this is not the muxe paradise.' These festivals are explicitly marketed to foreign tourists, making the exclusion directly visitor-facing. The state human-rights ombudsperson opened 34 discrimination investigations involving LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022. April 2025 reporting characterised Oaxaca as Mexico's fastest-growing tourist paradise but 'the most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community,' with incidents under investigation for possible municipal-police participation in regions where armed groups operate. Authorities responded by stepping up visitor security.

Countervailing: LGR since 2019, extended to 12+ in 2021, fully opened by a 2023 Supreme Court ruling. Traditional muxe recognition is culturally real (49th annual 'Auténticas Intrépidas Buscadoras del Peligro' vela). The positive and negative signals coexist: the formal legal framework is protective, but customary-exclusion enforcement at the exact events tourists attend, combined with the 'most dangerous' characterization, creates a specific travel risk.

Below the national 0.55 (−0.07). Versus Yucatán (no record, ~national), which has a 23-year uninterrupted Pride march and no documented counter-attacks, Oaxaca's tourist-facing exclusion and armed-group amplifier are materially worse. Versus CDMX (0.57), where the same high violence is met with a dedicated investigation unit and protocol, Oaxaca's violence is attributed partly to police participation and addressed by 'stepping up visitor security' rather than structural reform.
31927357B6525686063804.modelContext: Indigenous-majority, traditional communal governance (usos y costumbres) is socially conservative; muxe third-gender tradition in Juchitán is a documented local tolerance pocket.

31927357B1137737933275.name: Puebla
31927357B1137737933275.summary:
Puebla led the national statistics for 2025 with 7 recorded killings of LGBT+ people; trans women constituted 58.3% of all such killings nationwide that year, across at least 17 reporting states. Its LGR law (2021) imposed an 18-year-old requirement that the Supreme Court voided in March 2022, yet congress has still not corrected the text — legislative non-compliance with a final court ruling is itself a hostility signal directly relevant to a visitor whose documents need to match presentation.

No dedicated investigative machinery, no transfeminicide offence, no state-level enforcement data. The combination of top-of-table lethality and open defiance of the judiciary distinguishes Puebla from states that simply lack statutes; here a statute exists but the legislature actively refuses to conform it to a binding ruling.

Below the national 0.55 (−0.10). Versus CDMX (0.57), which also had high 2024–25 counts but created a transfeminicide unit and protocol within months, Puebla has neither the legal correction nor any enforcement innovation. Versus Estado de México (0.48), which also defies a SCOTUS ruling on recognition but at least has hate-crime provision art. 211 Sexies since 2021, Puebla has neither the court-compliance nor the criminal-law protection.
31927357B1137737933275.modelContext: Deep Catholic conservative heartland; large university city (Puebla/Buap) with a small scene.

1811400B57209440839078.name: Tripura
1811400B57209440839078.summary:
Tripura exhibits the country's clearest border-checkpoint pattern of profiling gender-nonconforming presentation as a suspicion trigger for foreign infiltration. Three mass police sweeps in five months (Aug–Nov 2024) at the Panisagar check post on the Agartala–Guwahati highway detained 15, 7, and 12 individuals respectively, with police reporting language explicitly framing trans identity as "disguised as third-gender" — a category of deception rather than personhood. The state shares an 856 km border with Bangladesh. These are named-state-actor operations with published counts, constituting a patterned enforcement practice directly facing any trans-presenting visitor crossing by land.

The deviation from the national 0.43 is substantial (−0.12): while India has no statute criminalising trans presence, Tripura's checkpoint regime converts gender-nonconforming appearance into an independently sufficient reason for detention and deportation proceedings. Compared to West Bengal (0.34), which shares the same script but records it in fewer, more isolated incidents, Tripura's three sweeps within 24-hour windows and the explicit "disguise" framing make it the most concentrated instance of this visitor-facing harm in the country.

Tripura does have a constituted transgender welfare board (one of only 12 states/UTs), but the RTI investigation found most boards to be "rudderless" with no compliance mechanism or real power — this institutional presence does not offset active police profiling at the border.
1811400B57209440839078.modelContext: Small northeastern state; documented violence rates high (general crime + instability); institutions thin — danger is general-lawlessness, not LGBT-targeted.

1811400B32673734874058.name: West Bengal
1811400B32673734874058.summary:
West Bengal replicates the Tripura checkpoint script: South Dinajpur police arrested a Bangladeshi transgender person for allegedly "infiltrating India," treating trans presentation as evidence of illegal entry rather than identity. The state shares a long Bangladesh border and falls within the same policing logic. West Bengal is also one of only three states recording cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 (3 of 7 nationally), indicating some legal infrastructure exists but also that trans-targeted crime is occurring at a detectable rate.

Against the national 0.43, West Bengal sits −0.09. The border profiling is visitor-facing and state-actor-driven, but the incidents are fewer and less concentrated than Tripura's triple-sweep pattern. Compared to Tripura (0.31), West Bengal's harm is a single documented arrest plus the broader infiltration framing rather than repeated mass operations; compared to Delhi (0.38), which shares the profiling language but also has India's strongest institutional trans presence, West Bengal lacks that offsetting civic infrastructure outside Kolkata.

A welfare board exists (one of 12 states/UTs with a constituted body), but per the RTI investigation it operates without a functioning policy framework. For a foreign visitor transiting the land border, the primary exposure is the same appearance-as-suspicion-trigger mechanism documented in Tripura.
1811400B32673734874058.modelContext: Kolkata: historic hijra visibility and first Indian trans-activism (1970s); Left-era institutions; but West Bengal political violence and police partisanship documented.

1811400B91946361694107.name: Punjab
1811400B91946361694107.summary:
Pride Amritsar cancelled its 27 April 2025 parade after "mounting resistance" from Sikh religious organisations, specifically the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht — the faith's highest temporal authority. Organisers cited religious-group opposition as the reason. Amritsar is the spiritual centre of Sikhism, and the Akal Takht exercises quasi-governmental power over public assembly within its sphere, making this a state-implicated suppression of trans public expression rather than a private dispute.

Against the national 0.43, Punjab sits −0.08. While the single-incident rule counsels caution, this event meets the exception: it is state-implicated (a named authority with effective governmental power compelled the cancellation), it was met with impunity (the event simply did not happen), and it directly suppresses the public visibility a visitor relies on for safety. Compared to Delhi (0.38), which also faces police profiling but maintains India's most visible trans civic presence, Punjab's suppression targets the civic presence itself. Compared to Tamil Nadu (0.53), where a court actively commended trans-affirming policy, Punjab demonstrates the inverse dynamic — religious authority vetoing trans assembly.

No Punjab-specific welfare board or trans-related statute deviation was identified beyond this event. The finding is narrow but material: a trans visitor attending a public gathering in Amritsar encounters a documented precedent of institutional suppression.
1811400B91946361694107.modelContext: Strong Sikh-traditional society; Chandigarh (shared capital) has an organized scene; emigration culture means families police gender hard, but violence is social, not state-driven.

1811400B21167269026319.name: Tamil Nādu
1811400B21167269026319.summary:
Tamil Nadu is India's most protective sub-national regime for trans visitors. It was the first state to introduce a transgender welfare policy (1995), maintains a dedicated Transgender Welfare Board within the Social Welfare & Women Empowerment Department, and adopted a comprehensive State Policy for Transgender Persons in 2025. On 4 August 2025, the Madras High Court (WP 7284 of 2021) expressly commended the policy as "a victory for transgender and intersex persons after their long struggle" — active judicial confirmation of executive protection is rare and meaningful for a visitor's institutional recourse. Tamil Nadu was also the sole state recording a Transgender Persons Act case in 2020 (1 of 1 nationally), indicating courts are engaged.

Against the national 0.43, Tamil Nadu sits +0.10. The state has a functioning (by comparison) policy apparatus, court validation, and the Thirunangai/Thirunambi administrative categories embedded in governance. Compared to Kerala (0.50), Tamil Nadu adds the explicit court commendation and longer institutional history; compared to Punjab (0.35), which saw a religious authority veto trans public assembly, Tamil Nadu's state machinery actively protects it. A complicating signal exists — Hindu transgender devotees in Madurai announced a fast in December 2025 over temple lamp-lighting decisions — but this reflects trans people as political actors in state governance, not state suppression of them.
1811400B21167269026319.modelContext: Chennai: thirunangai/aravani activism is India's most institutionalized trans organizing (Transgender Welfare Board first in India, 2008); temples-and-tradition culture has historic gender-variant roles; society conservative but state machinery protective.

1811400B45534780755480.name: Kerala
1811400B45534780755480.summary:
Kerala was the first state in India to adopt a dedicated Policy for Transgenders, with named welfare measures including an overseas scholarship scheme administered through the Social Justice Department. A constituted welfare board exists. Kerala is one of only three states recording cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 (2 of 7 nationally), indicating the legal machinery is at least operational and that trans-targeted incidents are being formally registered rather than ignored.

Against the national 0.43, Kerala sits +0.07. The policy infrastructure and scholarship scheme represent genuine state commitment to trans inclusion beyond the federal floor. Compared to Tamil Nadu (0.53), Kerala lacks the additional layer of active judicial endorsement (the Madras High Court commendation) and the longer institutional history since 1995, but its first-state policy status and operational board mark it clearly above the national norm. Compared to Assam (0.45), Kerala's protective framework is more developed and better documented.

For a visitor, the practical benefit is institutional visibility: a trans-presenting person in Kochi or urban Kerala encounters a governance structure that has codified recognition, though like most Indian states, city-level norms in Thiruvananthapuram or Kochi are far more protective than rural areas.
1811400B45534780755480.modelContext: India's highest social-development indicators; Kochi Queerala/Trans Pride organized; society matrilineal-legacy but publicly moralistic; institutions strong.

1811400B78322693766699.name: Assam
1811400B78322693766699.summary:
Assam recorded 2 of 7 national Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021, indicating some functioning legal infrastructure for trans-related complaints. The state is part of the Northeast border belt where the infiltration/Bangladeshi-detention script operates — the Panisagar raids run along the Assam–Agartala highway — though no Assam-specific checkpoint case was identified in this research pass. A constituted welfare board exists.

Against the national 0.43, Assam sits marginally +0.02. The positive signal is thin: recorded cases under the Trans Act could indicate either crimes happening or a legal system engaging with them, and the dossier frames the latter reading. The negative ambient signal (proximity to the Tripura/West Bengal border-profiling zone) is not offset by any Assam-specific protective policy comparable to Tamil Nadu or Kerala. Compared to West Bengal (0.34), Assam shares the border-belt exposure but lacks the documented trans-as-infiltration arrests; compared to Tripura (0.31), the absence of any named checkpoint operation in Assam is the key differentiator. The deviation is small and confidence is low.
1811400B78322693766699.modelContext: Guwahati: Northeast India's organized scene hub; Assamese society historically tolerant of gender variance (hijra-friendly festival traditions); institutions improving.

1811400B11231190780494.name: Uttar Pradesh
1811400B11231190780494.summary:
Uttar Pradesh hosts the most trans-visible public space in India: the Kinnar Akhara (trans/hijra monastic order) fielded a Mahamandaleshwar — one of its highest-ranking monks — leading ceremonial bathing at the Kumbh Mela in Prayagraj (Jan–Feb 2025), the world's largest religious gathering. A trans visitor at the Kumbh is inside an institutionally recognised religious hierarchy, not a marginalised underground. UP also has a constituted welfare board.

Against the national 0.43, UP sits +0.03. The Kinnar Akhara inclusion is visitor-facing, seasonal, and institutionally validated by the broader Akharas' governance structures. A counterweight exists — a single transgender woman, Kajal, was strangled in Kanpur (Aug 2025) during a robbery — but this is a lone incident with no patterned state-actor response and does not constitute a regional finding under the single-incident rule. Compared to Tamil Nadu (0.53), UP lacks a comprehensive policy framework or judicial endorsement; compared to Maharashtra (0.38), UP does not show the festival-entry religion-screening that creates outing mechanisms at public gatherings. The net positive is narrow and temporally concentrated.
1811400B11231190780494.modelContext: India's most populous, poorest-governed heartland; Lucknow/Kanpur historic hijra culture (nirvan community) coexists with severe police arbitrariness; rule of law weakest among major states.

1811400B70654311394581.name: Chhattīsgarh
1811400B70654311394581.summary:
Chhattisgarh mirrors Maharashtra's garba screening: in Bastar district, VHP and Bajrang Dal members objected to non-Hindu sponsors and participants at garba events, claiming damage to "cultural purity," creating the same ID-checked, religion-gated entry mechanism that outs gender-nonconforming visitors to informal enforcers. Unlike Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh has no constituted transgender welfare board (absent from the 12-state/UT list). Additionally, in November 2024 a transgender woman was shot dead in an abandoned quarry in a Rs 12 lakh contract killing over rival claims to a community leadership seat — a single incident with no sourced second instance, recorded for pattern awareness rather than as a decisive factor.

Against the national 0.43, Chhattisgarh sits −0.06. The combination of festival-entrance screening (visitor-facing, seasonal, outing mechanism) and the absence of any state welfare apparatus distinguishes it from Maharashtra (0.38), which carries the same screening but at least has a board. Compared to Tripura (0.31), whose harm is state-police-driven border detention, Chhattisgarh's exposure is community-organiser-driven at private-adjacent festivals and the violence is a single unresolved incident. The gap to the national score is modest and confidence moderate.
1811400B70654311394581.modelContext: Naxalite-insurgency zones in the south; weak governance; Raipur small scene.

14911670B7632012573600.name: Ceara
14911670B7632012573600.summary:
Ceará is the most consistent lethal hotspot for trans and travesti people in the Northeast: 11 killings in 2024 (3rd nationally, 1st in the region) and 8 in 2025 (tied for the highest state total in the country). Against a population of ~9 million this yields roughly 0.9 killings per million per year—more than double the national rate of ~0.38/million (80 / 213 M). The 2025 dossier further notes a concentration of Black victims in Ceará.

This places Ceará about 0.10 below the national 0.71. The deviation is driven by sustained, patterned lethal exposure rather than any legal distinction (the federal constitution and penal code apply uniformly). Compared with Minas Gerais (0.64), which matched Ceará's absolute 2025 count of 8, Minas Gerais' much larger population (~21 M) gives a per-capita rate at the national average, making Ceará the higher-risk state on a rate basis.

For a visibly trans visitor, the pattern matters: the killings are concentrated on young Black trans women in public space—precisely the exposure profile of a conspicuous traveller—and the consistency across two years signals an entrenched environment rather than a statistical blip.
14911670B7632012573600.modelContext: Fortaleza: large beach-tourism scene; drag culture visible; interior conservative.

14911670B91095571793858.name: Rio Granda do Norte
14911670B91095571793858.summary:
Rio Grande do Norte recorded zero trans killings in 2024 but jumped to 4 in 2025—the sharpest deterioration in the ANTRA dataset. Against a population of ~3.5 million, four cases yields approximately 1.14 killings per million per year, the highest per-capita rate among all 27 units in 2025 and roughly three times the national figure of ~0.38/million. The dossier cautions against reading a single-year zero as safety and notes the volatility.

This rate-driven exposure puts RN about 0.11 below the national 0.71. Compared with Ceará (0.61), RN's absolute count is lower (4 vs 8) but the per-capita risk is actually higher; the deviation from national is therefore slightly larger than one might expect from the raw numbers. The state sits within the Northeast bloc that accounted for 38 of 80 national killings in 2025.

No state-level statutory restriction or unique legal finding applies; the risk is purely a violence-rate signal. For a visitor, the small absolute numbers mean a single incident dramatically shifts perception, and the volatility suggests the environment can turn rapidly.
14911670B91095571793858.modelContext: Natal: tourism coast with visible scene; interior traditional.

14911670B97385369352280.name: Paraiba
14911670B97385369352280.summary:
Paraíba recorded 4 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the same absolute count as Rio Grande do Norte. Against a population of ~4 million this yields approximately 1.0 per million per year—well above the national rate of ~0.38/million and among the highest in the federation. The state is part of the Northeast bloc that absorbed 38 of 80 national killings (47.5%) in 2025.

The per-capita rate places Paraíba roughly 0.09 below the national 0.71. Compared with Alagoas (0.68), which had 2 killings in a similar population (~3.3 M, rate ~0.61/million), Paraíba's absolute count is double and its rate higher, reflecting the broader Northeast concentration on a smaller denominator.

No Paraíba-specific legal or ordinance evidence was found; the deviation is driven entirely by the violence dataset. The victim profile—young, Black, poor, Northeastern—concentrates risk on individuals who present visibly in public space.
14911670B97385369352280.modelContext: João Pessoa modest scene; small traditional northeastern state; documented violence rates high but not LGBT-specific in pattern.

14911670B44044837234259.name: Minas Gerais
14911670B44044837234259.summary:
Minas Gerais ranked 2nd nationally in 2024 with 12 killings and tied for the top in 2025 with 8 (matching Ceará). Against a population of ~21 million, the 2025 rate of ~0.38/million sits at the national average, but the consistency of appearing in the top two every year signals a structurally elevated environment compared with states that fluctuate. The 2024 total of 12 placed it behind only São Paulo.

These factors put Minas Gerais about 0.07 below the national 0.71. Compared with Ceará (0.61), which matched the same 2025 absolute count on a much smaller population, Minas Gerais' per-capita exposure is roughly half—so the deviation is more moderate. Compared with São Paulo (no deviation recorded), which led the 2024 count at 16 but fell sharply in 2025, Minas Gerais' consistency across both years is the distinguishing risk factor.

No state-specific legal restriction or unique ordinance was identified. The risk for a visitor is violence-exposure, patterned over two years, in a large interior state where the 68%-outside-capitals finding of the 2024 dossier implies added danger away from Belo Horizonte.
14911670B44044837234259.modelContext: Belo Horizonte: large established scene; Minas is Brazil's swing-state heartland — socially traditional interior, urban institutions strong.

14911670B2612452665424.name: Pernambuco
14911670B2612452665424.summary:
Pernambuco recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, placing it in the second tier behind Ceará/Minas Gerais. Against a population of ~9.4 million this yields roughly 0.74 per million per year—nearly double the national rate. Crucially, the state hosts the major tourist corridor of Recife and Olinda, so the violence concentration directly overlaps with visitor traffic and visible trans presence in public coastal spaces.

The rate and tourism overlap put Pernambuco about 0.07 below the national 0.71. Compared with Bahia (0.65), which also recorded 7 killings in 2025, Bahia's larger population (~15 M) gives a lower per-capita rate of ~0.47/million; Pernambuco's risk density is therefore somewhat higher despite the identical absolute count, and both states share the visitor-coast exposure.

No Pernambuco-specific legal restriction or ordinance was found. The deviation is violence-driven and location-dependent: a trans visitor staying in Recife's centre or the Olida historic district is in the same geography where the killings cluster.
14911670B2612452665424.modelContext: Recife: established scene and strong university activism; interior (sertão) traditional.

14911670B19428866735507.name: Bahia
14911670B19428866735507.summary:
Bahia recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the same absolute count as Pernambuco and the second tier nationally. Against a population of ~15 million the rate is approximately 0.47 per million per year, above the national 0.38/million but below Ceará and Pernambuco. Bahia's coast—Salvador, the beaches—draws substantial tourist traffic, and the violence data overlaps with visitor areas.

These findings place Bahia about 0.06 below the national 0.71. Compared with Pernambuco (0.64), which matched the absolute count on a smaller population (higher rate), Bahia's per-capita exposure is somewhat lower, justifying the small positive delta. Compared with the national average, Bahia sits high in the danger range, driven by Northeast-region concentration (38 of 80 killings in 2025) rather than by any local legal distinction.

No Bahia-specific ordinance or statutory restriction was identified. The risk is a violence gradient within the broader Northeast pattern, with tourism overlap raising visitor exposure above what the per-capita rate alone suggests.
14911670B19428866735507.modelContext: Salvador: Brazil's Afro-Brazilian cultural capital with deep gender-nonconformist traditions (transformismo culture); but Bahia's interior is socially conservative and state violence rates high.

14911670B85657526756793.name: Rio de Jeneiro
14911670B85657526756793.summary:
Rio de Janeiro recorded only 3 trans killings in 2025 (a low rate of ~0.18/million against a population of ~17 M), well below the national average. However, two distinct visitor-facing signals pull the score modestly below the national 0.71: a documented extortion pattern in Niterói and a tourist-targeting scam in Copacabana.

In January–February 2026, multiple trans sex workers in central Niterói reported a two-year coercive regime: a man claiming militia and public-agent connections forced them to pay R$120 per week each and had 'almost strangled three of the girls.' The alleged extorter was an ex-employee of Niterói city hall, arrested in 'Operação Ronda Sumbria' by the 76ª DP, and remanded in pre-trial custody. The institutional response was mixed—arrests and dismissal occurred, but the racket operated under the appearance of state backing for roughly two years before intervention. Trans council member Benny Briolly brought the case to the Public Ministry.

Separately, in Copacabana the tourist police (Deat) arrested two trans women caught extorting a Norwegian tourist with threats to circulate intimate videos—a documented, visitor-facing scam vector. The killing rate is low, but the coercive pattern with state implication and the tourist-targeting scam justify a deviation of about 0.03 below national. Compared with São Paulo (no deviation), Rio's risk is qualitative rather than numerical.
14911670B85657526756793.modelContext: Rio: visible beach-culture scene (Ipanema/Copacabana); state police violence extreme but not LGBT-targeted specifically; favela governance (milícia/trafico) imposes local moral codes in places.

14911670B6484683145874.name: Goias
14911670B6484683145874.summary:
Goiás recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, placing it in the mid-band alongside Maranhão and Pará. Against a population of ~7.2 million the rate is approximately 0.69 per million per year, about 1.8× the national rate of 0.38/million. Goiás sits on the Cerrado agricultural frontier, and the dossier notes that 68% of 2024 killings occurred outside state capitals—in interior towns where a visitor's exposure may be harder to mitigate.

The rate and absence of any mitigating legal or institutional finding place Goiás about 0.04 below the national 0.71. Compared with Minas Gerais (0.64), which had 8 killings in 2025, Goiás' lower absolute count partly reflects a smaller population, but the per-capita gap (0.69 vs 0.38/million) is directionally consistent with a moderate deviation. No Goiás-specific ordinance or statutory restriction was identified.
14911670B6484683145874.modelContext: Goiânia: agribusiness heartland, socially conservative (evangelical belt); scene small but exists.

14911670B41041569544971.name: Maranhao
14911670B41041569544971.summary:
Maranhão recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the same absolute count as Goiás and Pará. Against a population of ~7.1 million the rate is approximately 0.70 per million per year, nearly double the national average. Maranhão is one of the poorest states in the federation, and the dossier's victim profile—young, Black, poor, Northeastern—maps directly onto the state's demographics, suggesting the killings are not incidental but patterned along the structural inequalities that make trans visibility most dangerous.

The rate and poverty-driven vulnerability place Maranhão about 0.04 below the national 0.71. Compared with Ceará (0.61), which shares the Northeast concentration but recorded 8 killings on a smaller population (rate ~0.89/million), Maranhão's risk is somewhat lower but in the same directional band. No unit-specific legal or ordinance evidence was found.
14911670B41041569544971.modelContext: São Luís: traditional; among Brazil's poorest institutions.

14911670B48776179681147.name: Para
14911670B48776179681147.summary:
Pará recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, matching the Goiás/Maranhão band. Against a population of ~8.7 million the rate is approximately 0.57 per million per year, above the national 0.38/million. Pará spans the Amazon region, where the 68%-outside-capitals finding means interior municipal exposure is difficult to assess and infrastructure for protection is thinner.

The above-national rate and geographic risk-concentration place Pará about 0.04 below the national 0.71. Compared with Ceará (0.61), which had 8 killings on ~9 million (rate ~0.89/million), Pará is less severe on a per-capita basis, but the Amazonian interior geography amplifies the difficulty of accessing help after an incident for a visitor. No Pará-specific legal or ordinance finding was identified.
14911670B48776179681147.modelContext: Belém: established scene; interior Amazon under weak governance.

14911670B9724590061217.name: Alagoas
14911670B9724590061217.summary:
Alagoas recorded 2 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025. Against a population of ~3.3 million the rate is approximately 0.61 per million per year, above the national average but below the Ceará/Paraíba/Rio Grande do Norte cluster. Alagoas is part of the Northeast bloc that absorbed 38 of 80 national killings in 2025, so the unit sits in a region of elevated violence even though its own absolute count is modest.

The above-national rate and regional concentration justify a deviation of about 0.03 below the national 0.71. Compared with Paraíba (0.62), which recorded 4 killings on a similar population (rate ~1.0/million), Alagoas is materially less severe, and the small absolute number (2) means a single case would shift the rate dramatically. No unit-specific legal restriction or enforcement finding was identified.
14911670B9724590061217.modelContext: Maceió: tourism coast; Alagoas historically among the highest violence rates; conservative interior.

14911670B2082355341666.name: Mato Grosso
14911670B2082355341666.summary:
Mato Grosso recorded 3 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025. Against a population of ~3.6 million the rate is approximately 0.83 per million per year—more than double the national rate of 0.38/million. The state sits on the Cerrado/agribusiness frontier, an area where the 68%-outside-capitals pattern means small-town exposure is relevant for a visitor travelling beyond Cuiabá.

The elevated per-capita rate places Mato Grosso about 0.02 below the national 0.71, the minimum threshold for a record. The deviation is modest because 3 cases on a small population is statistically fragile and no qualitative incident, ordinance, or enforcement evidence was found beyond the ANTRA count. Compared with Goiás (0.67), which recorded 5 killings on ~7.2 million (rate ~0.69/million), Mato Grosso's per-capita figure is actually higher, but the smaller absolute count and absence of corroborating detail justify a smaller deviation.
14911670B2082355341666.modelContext: Cuiabá: agribusiness frontier conservatism; institutions thin.

14911670B84195346134564.name: Distrito Federal
14911670B84195346134564.summary:
The Distrito Federal recorded 2 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, a low absolute count for a major metropolitan area. Brasília is the seat of the STF, the national protective apparatus, and the offices of human-rights bodies; ANTRA's own Dossiê is compiled and reported from DF desks. The capital hosts international diplomatic missions and NGO infrastructure that raise the visibility and institutional cost of anti-trans violence.

These factors justify a modest positive deviation of about 0.02 above the national 0.71. Compared with São Paulo (0.71, no deviation), which also leads in institutional capacity but recorded 4 killings in 2025 and 16 in 2024, the DF's lower absolute numbers and concentration of protective infrastructure make it marginally safer for a visitor. The 2 killings against ~3 million population give a rate of ~0.67/million—above the national average in per-capita terms—so the positive deviation is qualitative (institutional visibility, international presence) rather than purely numerical.
14911670B84195346134564.modelContext: Brasília: institutions, diplomacy, organized scene; planned city with anonymity limits but strong institutional presence.

10402087B89016843004490.name: Sachsen
10402087B89016843004490.summary:
Sachsen is the epicentre of both legislative hostility and organised street violence against queer events in Germany. In 2024–2025, Pride events across the state were disrupted by coordinated far-right counter-mobilisations: a mob of more than 700 neo-Nazis assembled at the Bautzen parade (summer 2024, the season's largest organised counter-protest, alongside nine further pride-event incidents statewide); in Döbeln (September 2025), a simultaneous counter-march through town produced seven criminal offences and a formal investigation after a public Hitler salute; in Dresden (2025), neo-Nazis attempted to disrupt the parade with a counter-protest. The state also co-authored the Bundesrat initiative (with Sachsen-Anhalt and Thüringen) to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG), an organised multi-state attempt to roll back trans self-ID rights.

Mitigating factors: police protection let all events proceed without physical harm to attendees; the Bautzen 2025 parade ran under heavy police presence; Leipzig and Dresden's inner neighbourhoods remain comparatively safe. The violence pattern is concentrated in small and mid-sized towns and rural areas rather than the major urban centres.

Deviation: −0.16 from the national score (0.71). The spread reflects the only state combining a multi-city pattern of organised street attacks with active legislative hostility toward trans rights. Below Brandenburg (0.64), whose violence is concentrated in one city (Cottbus) with a positive Staatsschutz response; below Sachsen-Anhalt (0.63) which shares the SBGG initiative but lacks documented street attacks. The urban/rural caveat applies: this score reflects the state-wide pattern, not Leipzig's everyday environment.
10402087B89016843004490.modelContext: Dresden/Leipzig have real scenes (Leipzig notably alternative-friendly), but rural Saxony is AfD-core territory with the highest documented anti-LGBT incident density in Germany; police protection functions but social hostility is organized.

25490228B14384488423733.name: Comunitat Valenciana
25490228B14384488423733.summary:
The Comunitat Valenciana holds a dedicated integral law on the right to identity and gender expression (Llei de 7 d'abril, integral del reconeixement del dret a la identitat i expressió de gènere) alongside a general LGTBI-protection statute, making it one of only two communities (with Madrid) to have enacted legislation in both the trans-specific and general-LGTBI-equality categories. Unlike Madrid, Valencia has not amended or narrowed its provisions. The statutory framework supports institutional response channels for a visitor encountering discrimination.

No incident data, enforcement action, or negative visitor-facing finding was located for this community in the research pass. Valencia city carries a visible and well-established LGBTQ community with dedicated infrastructure. The divergence from national is modest and rests on the statutory-completeness evidence.

Vs national (0.88): +0.03, reflecting the presence of a dual-category legislative framework (gender identity + LGTBI equality) that is active and unrevised. Vs Madrid (0.83), which shares the dual-category structure but actively rolled back its provisions in 2023, Valencia's position is clearly safer. Vs Castilla y León (0.81), which has no law at all, the gap is 0.10 points driven entirely by the presence versus absence of statutory infrastructure.
25490228B14384488423733.modelContext: Valencia/Benidorm: large scene plus Europe's biggest LGBT tourism enclave (Sitges-adjacent culture); regional law explicitly protective.

19177384B97722443848736.name: Buenos Aires
19177384B97722443848736.summary:
Buenos Aires Province carries the strongest sub-national negative signal in Argentina: the federal human-rights ombudsman's 2016 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents acts of violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police—or by third parties under police cover—against trans and travesti people during operations in La Plata, Mar del Plata and Esteban Echeverría, carried out under "preventive policing" frameworks. Academic legal analysis (CELS CEDAW shadow report; UNLP/Pensamiento Penal) confirms that after the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security forces increased use of drug-law prosecution (devolved to provincial justice in 2005) and street-offence law as the operative instrument for indirect criminalisation of travesti/trans identity—a patterned, state-implicated escalation with impunity.

The deviation from the national score (0.58) is −0.05. No other province has a comparable volume of multi-source, patterned enforcement documentation reaching the UN treaty-body system. The evidence is not a single incident but a documented operational framework (drug-law devolution + anti-narcotics security policy) that measurably increased police persecution of trans women. Protective institutions coexist—the provincial defensoría maintains a 2024 registry-rectification guide and documents discrimination caseloads—but these are resident-facing and do not offset the visitor-facing exposure to arbitrary detention during any police stop.

Compared with Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires (0.55), the Province lacks CABA's tribunal contravencional judicial-oversight structure and anti-discrimination apparatus; its police-judge model under the código de faltas gives less post-detention review. Compared with the silent majority of provinces (national score), the difference is one of documented pattern rather than statutory hostility—no BA law criminalises gender identity, but enforcement practice does the work.
19177384B97722443848736.modelContext: Buenos Aires Province (conurbano): working-class periphery — visibility carries more risk than in CABA; police (Bonaerense) historically brutal and corrupt; La Plata and Mar del Plata (tourism, established scene) are the province's safer urban pockets.

17162690B44985096553766.name: Subcarpathian Voivodeship
17162690B44985096553766.summary:
Subcarpathian (Podkarpackie) is the epicentre and last holdout of Poland's "LGBT-ideology-free" resolution wave. It was one of five voivodeships adopting a regional anti-LGBT declaration (repealed 20 September 2021 only after the European Commission threatened to freeze its regional development funds), and its Łańcut county held Poland's final surviving anti-LGBT charter of the family until its extraordinary-session repeal on 24 April 2025—six years after the phenomenon began. The capital, Rzeszów, saw its mayor Tadeusz Ferenc outright ban the 2019 Equality March on security grounds; the district court later overturned the ban and the march proceeded, but the executive intent to exclude a visible LGBTQ public presence is on the record.

The resolutions were never criminal statutes, but the repeal was extrinsic (EU funding leverage) rather than a change in local attitudes, meaning the de facto social climate that produced them persists. For a visitor, the practical exposure is being visibly trans at a public event in an eastern Podkarpackie town where the local authority resisted all external pressure until 2025.

Score of 0.42 sits 0.10 below the national 0.52. Well below Łódź (0.48), which also carried a voivodeship-level resolution but produced neither a march ban nor a five-year institutional holdout. This is the deepest sub-national negative in Poland's dossier.
17162690B44985096553766.modelContext: Rzeszów/Podkarpacie: Poland's most religiously conservative voivodeship — highest church attendance, most gminy anti-LGBT resolutions, border-traditional culture; scene exists only in Rzeszów, discreetly.

17162690B23777949290372.name: Podlaskie Voivodeship
17162690B23777949290372.summary:
Podlaskie saw Poland's most violent assault on a public LGBTQ event: at the 20 July 2019 Białystok Equality March, roughly 1,000 marchers were attacked by thousands of far-right and football-hooligan groups who attempted to block the route. Police detained 25 people; 32 counter-demonstrations had been registered that day, including a prayer vigil at the Cathedral Basilica. In the run-up, Archbishop Tadeusz Wojda had a proclamation read in every church across the region. The surrounding Białystok County had been declared an LGBT-free zone in 2019, though the city itself did not adopt one, and its mayor questioned whether the march was "needed" while the PiS city council filed a motion to stop it.

The state's protective response improved materially: at the fourth Equality March (28 September 2024), ~300 participants were escorted by 500 police officers and the Podlaskie police reported zero incidents. This is positive evidence under the single-incident rule (institutional learning, proportionate deployment), but it does not erase the 2019 pattern—organised mass violence met with a partial 25-person detention response, embedded in a documented church-and-county mobilisation infrastructure.

Score of 0.44 sits 0.08 below the national 0.52. Slightly above Subcarpathian (0.42), which lacked Podlaskie's demonstrable five-year improvement in state protection, but below Masovian (0.56), where the institutional machinery runs the other way.
17162690B23777949290372.modelContext: Białystok 2019 Equality March mob violence is Poland's most infamous incident — the northeast is the country's most nationalistically conservative region; institutions protective on paper, socially hostile in practice.

17162690B69262761487853.name: Lublin Voivodeship
17162690B69262761487853.summary:
Lubelskie carried a voivodeship-level "LGBT-free" resolution from 2020 until its 20 September 2021 repeal under European Commission funding pressure. Its municipality of Świdnik (population ~40,000) was the first local authority in all of Poland to adopt an anti-LGBT resolution (March 2019, "against homopropaganda, LGBT ideology and the early sexualisation of Polish children"), and its deputy council chair explained the act explicitly as opposition to Warsaw's LGBT+ Declaration signed a month earlier. Świdnik became the template copied by roughly 100 authorities nationwide.

The resolution is now formally gone, but as with other eastern voivodeships the repeal was coerced rather than converted—the underlying civic mobilisation that produced Poland's first-ever anti-LGBT charter persists as a de facto signal. No march violence or ban is documented at the voivodeship scale beyond the general resolution-era hostility.

Score of 0.45 sits 0.07 below the national 0.52. Above Subcarpathian (0.42), which additionally produced a mayoral march ban and held out until 2025, and above Podlaskie (0.44), where the 2019 coordinated mass assault adds a violence dimension absent in Lublin. Below Małopolska (0.48), which pairs its resolution history with Kraków's clearly positive institutional trajectory.
17162690B69262761487853.modelContext: Lublin: east Poland's most conservative major region (church influence strongest); Equality Marches held under police protection against counter-demonstrations.

17162690B67655395900928.name: Lesser Poland Voivodeship
17162690B67655395900928.summary:
Małopolska adopted a voivodeship-level "LGBT-ideology-free" resolution in 2020, repealed on 20 September 2021 under EU funding pressure, placing it in the same five-region configuration as the eastern belt. The regional declaration carried the same intent as its siblings: to exclude a visible public LGBTQ presence from the voivodeship's civic space.

Within the same unit, however, Kraków—the capital and Poland's second city—has moved decisively the other direction. In May 2024 newly elected mayor Aleksander Miszalski announced he would become the first Kraków mayor ever to attend the city's LGBT Equality March and would fly a rainbow flag at city hall. His predecessor Jacek Majchrowski (2002–2024) had only become an honorary patron of the march in 2021 and never attended. For a visitor in Kraków's old town, the operative institutional signal is the mayor's public presence, not the repealed voivodeship document.

Score of 0.48 sits 0.04 below the national 0.52: the resolution history pulls it down, Kraków's positive trajectory prevents a deeper drop. Above Lublin (0.45), where no equivalent capital-city counter-signal exists, and well above Subcarpathian (0.42), where the capital actively banned a march. Below Masovian (0.56), where Warsaw's institutional machinery works continuously in the visitor's favour.
17162690B67655395900928.modelContext: Kraków: major scene and Equality Marches, university cosmopolitanism; but surrounding Małopolska countryside is among Poland's most traditional-Catholic (gminy anti-LGBT resolution heartland).

17162690B86810837764805.name: Łódź Voivodeship
17162690B86810837764805.summary:
Łódzkie was one of the five voivodeships that formally adopted an "anti-LGBT ideology" resolution by mid-2020, placing approximately one-third of Poland's territory under declarations whose stated purpose was to exclude LGBTQ public events. It sits in the PiS-vote heartland belt running east of the Łódź metro area. The resolution was struck down or repealed in the 2021 wave following EU Commission funding threats.

No march ban, coordinated attack, or county-level holdout comparable to Subcarpathian's Łańcut (2025) or Podlaskie's Białystok County is documented for Łódzkie. The sub-national finding is the regional resolution itself and its location in the eastern conservative bloc; the practical visitor-facing exposure is the general social climate of that bloc rather than a specific enforcement or violence event.

Score of 0.48 sits 0.04 below the national 0.52, matching Małopolska (0.48) for having a voivodeship-level resolution without an additional capital-city positive counterweight or a documented enforcement/violence episode. Well above Subcarpathian (0.42) and Podlaskie (0.44), both of which carry specific ban or assault evidence.
17162690B86810837764805.modelContext: No distinctive sub-national knowledge from the model. Treat this unit as inheriting the national climate exactly — including its social conservatism, informal norms and unreported violence. Under-documentation here is not safety, and it is not danger either.

17162690B20834640531728.name: Świętokrzyskie Voivodeship
17162690B20834640531728.summary:
Świętokrzyskie was the fifth of the voivodeships adopting a regional "anti-LGBT ideology" resolution by June 2020, completing the configuration that at peak covered about a third of national territory across roughly 100 municipalities and five regions. Located in the same eastern conservative bloc as Łódzkie and Lubelskie, its resolution was annulled or repealed in the 2020–2021 court-and-EU-pressure wave.

No march ban, violence episode, or holdout municipality comparable to the Subcarpathian or Podlaskie findings is documented at the voivodeship scale. The visitor-facing signal is the regional declaration's intent to exclude LGBTQ public presence and the social climate of the PiS heartland belt; the formal legal document is now absent.

Score of 0.48 sits 0.04 below the national 0.52, identical to Łódzkie (0.48) on shared evidence: both are resolution-carrying voivodeships in the eastern bloc without unit-specific enforcement or violence findings beyond the declaration itself. Above Lublin (0.45), which additionally contains Świdnik, Poland's first-ever anti-LGBT municipal resolution.
17162690B20834640531728.modelContext: No distinctive sub-national knowledge from the model. Treat this unit as inheriting the national climate exactly — including its social conservatism, informal norms and unreported violence. Under-documentation here is not safety, and it is not danger either.

17162690B84565288021286.name: Masovian Voivodeship
17162690B84565288021286.summary:
Masovian, anchored by Warsaw, is the institutional counterweight to Poland's eastern resolution belt. On 6 February 2024, Warsaw's Voivodeship Administrative Court repealed the last remaining "against LGBT ideology" document in the country. Warsaw is the origin point of the progressive response: in February 2019 Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski signed a 12-point LGBT+ Declaration (security, education, culture, sport, employment; drawn up with LGBT NGOs, including an intervention hostel and school "lighthouse keeper" projects), which provoked the first anti-LGBT municipal resolution (Świdnik, March 2019) as an explicit counter-reaction. The voivodeship-level court system headquartered in Warsaw carried out the annulment work that dismantled the resolution network nationally.

The unit's dark stain is historical: in November 2005 then-mayor Lech Kaczyński banned the Parada Równości, and the ECtHR in Bączkowski and Others v. Poland (2007) ruled the ban violated Articles 11, 13, and 14 ECHR. This is 20 years past and has not been repeated; the current institutional trajectory is clearly positive.
