76434192B92524600968894.summary:
Mpumalanga is geographically attributable as the institutional home of the National House of Traditional Leaders' (NHTL) formal campaign against constitutional equality for queer people. The NHTL—South Africa's official body of tribal chiefs—met at Hazyview, Mpumalanga, and resolved that "traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts," and separately asked Parliament to review the constitutional clause protecting against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Daily Maverick commentary identifies this NHTL lobbying, together with the chair of the Constitutional Review Committee, as precisely the mechanism that "intensifies prejudice and hatred" and fuels homophobic violence—an identified official-climate pathway, not merely a statement.

The dossier notes this evidence dates from 2012–2016 and should be treated as durable climate rather than current enacted policy. No provincial statute, no enforcement against a visitor, and no trans-specific incident series is documented. Mpumalanga is not listed in the former-Bantustan traditional-court geography; its risk signal is the formal institutional position taken on its soil, not a parallel legal system operating on visitors. South Africa's Constitution, PEPUDA, and the Hate Crime framework remain uniform and protective at the national level.

The score is 0.04 below the national 0.69. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), Mpumalanga sits higher because KZN adds both a retrieved township queerphobia study and the Zulu king / CONTRALESA episode with an ongoing traditional-court jurisdiction question; Mpumalanga's finding is one resolution and its subsequent lobbying, geographically located but not jurisdictionally operationalised against visitors. vs. Western Cape (0.72), the gap is driven by the absence of a metro NGO belt and the NHTL's public rejection of the equality clause versus the Cape's institutional visibility. vs. Gauteng (0.71), Mpumalanga lacks the representative hate-crime research infrastructure that signals an active civil-society response environment.
76434192B92524600968894.modelContext: Lowveld tourism (Kruger-adjacent) envelope in reserves vs traditional rural society outside; institutions thin.

76434192B37104984973577.name: Limpopo
76434192B37104984973577.summary:
Limpopo has the highest density of functioning traditional authority in South Africa, making the parallel customary-law jurisdiction most consequential here. HRW's analysis of the traditional-courts legislation (enacted as the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act 3 of 2019) is explicit that it "establishes a separate legal system for people living in the former Bantustans" and "threatens to undermine this security for millions of South Africans living in rural areas," "particularly for the exercise of gender and sexual rights," because chiefs and traditional courts adjudicate personal-status and morality-adjacent matters under customary law with a consent presumption running against the individual. The Act was declared constitutionally invalid in Mogale (ConCourt, 30 May 2023) but validity suspended and extended two years for Parliament to pass a replacement (TKLB, delayed 2023 and 2025).

No provincial trans-specific incident series was retrievable in English sources; this is a jurisdictional finding, not an incident finding. No statute criminalises a visitor's expression, no arrests are documented, and no religious criminal law operates here. The risk to a discovered/outed visitor is that in a rural Limpopo context the local moral authority is a chief's court, not a metro court with an LGBTQ+-trained prosecutor—and the customary-law adjudication of gender/sexuality has historically run against the individual.

The score is 0.04 below the national 0.69. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), Limpopo sits higher because KZN pairs the jurisdictional risk with a retrieved field study of township queerphobic violence AND the Zulu king / CONTRALESA episode; Limpopo's finding is purely the density of the parallel system without a documented trans incident. vs. North West (0.65), the two are comparable: both are former-Bantustan jurisdictions where traditional courts bite, but North West also has a 2010 provincial hate-crime study giving it a data-presence signal. vs. Western Cape (0.72), the gap is metro-institution vs. customary-authority geography. The dossier's under-reporting caveat means the absence of incidents here is not confirmation of safety.
76434192B37104984973577.modelContext: Most rural province; traditional Venda/Pedi authority strong; documented anti-LGBT sentiment high in rural surveys; institutions thinnest.

76434192B85643022077130.name: North West
76434192B85643022077130.summary:
North West sits squarely in the former-Bantustan geography where the traditional-courts jurisdiction is most extensive following the Bantustan-era map: HRW's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies these areas as a "separate legal system" whose adjudication of gender and sexual matters under customary law with a consent presumption against the individual constitutes the principal sub-national legal divergence in South Africa. The Act was declared invalid in Mogale (2023) but suspended and extended; the replacement Bill (TKLB) has been delayed. No province has religious criminal law; no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here.

North West is also one of only three provinces with its own representative hate-crime prevalence study (2010, noted in GALA's review alongside Gauteng and Western Cape), giving it a data-presence signal: incidents against queer people here are, historically, more likely to appear in research rather than only in the "dark figure" of unreported crime that characterises most provinces. No trans-specific incident series was found. The 2010 study covers gay and lesbian people; its relevance to a trans visitor is as a proxy for reporting culture and the volume of anti-queer violence in a traditional-authority-heavy province.

The score is 0.04 below the national 0.69. vs. Limpopo (0.65), the two share the former-Bantustan customary-authority finding at similar magnitude; North West's additional 2010 data presence does not raise it above Limpopo because the study documents violence prevalence rather than institutional response capacity. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), North West sits higher because KZN adds a retrieved township queerphobia study and the Zulu king / CONTRALESA official alignment against queer people; North West has the jurisdictional risk without a comparable named-authority statement. vs. Western Cape (0.72) and Gauteng (0.71), the gap reflects metro institutional functioning versus rural customary-authority geography. The dossier's under-reporting caveat applies equally: a province with more recorded hate crime may simply have better reporting than more danger.
76434192B85643022077130.modelContext: Rustenburg mining belt — migrant-labor hostels, traditional Tswana authority, weak institutions; low salience but low protection.

76434192B98113213215773.name: Eastern Cape
76434192B98113213215773.summary:
The Eastern Cape is listed among the former-Bantustan provinces where traditional-court jurisdiction operates—HRW's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies the rural gender/sexual-rights exposure under customary adjudication—but no trans-specific incident, statute, enforcement action, or institutional statement was found for this province. The dossier states plainly: "Free State and Eastern Cape have no trans-specific source at all." Provincial violence against women and girls is severe (multiple 2025 mass-casualty killings in Gqeberha), but arrests followed each incident (four suspects for the May 2025 killings, four for the June 2025 burning of teenagers at KwaNobuhle, charges against a police officer for the July 2025 killings at Gordon Terrace), and none of the victims is identified as trans. The arrests represent a functioning—if strained—state-response mechanism, which is a small positive against the backdrop of extreme national violent-crime rates.

For a visitor, the practical exposure is the general South African violent-crime baseline (national, priced into the 0.69) plus the township-and-rural customary-authority axis where a visibly gender-nonconforming person outside the metro NGO belt is more likely to encounter a chief's moral adjudication than a magistrate's court. No province-level ban, no enforcement against expression, no religious criminal law. The Constitutional Court's Mogale invalidity of the TKLA and the suspended replacement reduce but do not eliminate the parallel-system concern.

The score is 0.02 below the national 0.69. vs. Limpopo (0.65) and North West (0.65), the Eastern Cape sits higher because its traditional-authority density is lower (the dossier groups Limpopo/North West as the provinces where "traditional-court jurisdiction actually bites" most strongly), and the 2025 arrests demonstrate at least nominally functioning state enforcement in the metro (Gqeberha). vs. Gauteng (0.71) and Western Cape (0.72), the gap reflects the absence of a metro NGO/prosecutor belt and the rural customary-authority geography. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), the Eastern Cape's lower deviation from national reflects the absence of a retrieved trans-specific study or royal/CONTRALESA episode in this province.
76434192B98113213215773.modelContext: Most rural and traditional Xhosa heartland (initiation-school culture strongly gender-normative); documented violence high; institutions weakest; Nelson Mandela Bay modest scene.

76434192B69392740373411.name: Gauteng
76434192B69392740373411.summary:
Gauteng—where Johannesburg and Pretoria sit—is the best-documented and best-resourced province for an outed trans visitor. It hosts the only representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in South Africa (OUT LGBT Well-being, 2003/04), establishing prevalence, consequences, and contributing factors and signalling an active civil-society and research environment that can respond to incidents. GALA's companion review confirms that only three such studies have ever been done nationally (Gauteng, KZN, Western Cape 2003; North West 2010), placing Gauteng in the tier where evidence, reporting infrastructure, and NGO visibility exist. The HSRC/Global Pride Study analysis names the provincial paradox directly: internationally recognised legal protections coexist with "pervasive violence and discrimination" driven by "gender identity, visibility and health status," meaning Gauteng's courts and NGOs operate alongside genuine risk—but the operating courts and NGOs are the variable that matters for a visitor who is discovered.

For a foreign visitor, the practical difference is institutional: in Gauteng's metro belt, an incident is more likely to be handled by a police station with access to PEPUDA-trained prosecutors and LGBT-aware NGOs than by a chief's court or a township crowd. No province-specific ban, statute, or enforcement action exists. South Africa's constitutional protections (enumeration of sexual orientation and gender identity, PEPUDA, Hate Crime framework) apply uniformly; Gauteng's contribution is that the enforcement machinery behind them is most visible and accessible here. The under-reporting caveat cuts both ways: a province with more recorded hate crime is likelier to have better reporting than more danger.

The score is 0.02 above the national 0.69. vs. Western Cape (0.72), Gauteng sits marginally lower because the Western Cape (Cape Town) has the highest public visibility and the strongest NGO infrastructure per capita, while Gauteng's violence volume—acknowledged in the HSRC analysis—is higher. vs. Limpopo (0.65) and KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), the gap of 0.06–0.08 reflects metro-institutional functioning (courts, prosecutors, reporting) versus the township-and-rural customary-authority environment where the state's response is mediated by a chief's moral adjudication. vs. Northern Cape (0.64), the gap reflects the presence of a 20-year reporting and NGO infrastructure against a single-incident province with no comparable civil-
76434192B69392740373411.modelContext: Johannesburg/Pretoria: South Africa's economic heart — deepest scene infrastructure, organized NGOs (Iranti, GALA legacy), Constitutional Court jurisprudence world-leading; township violence coexists with Sandton/Soweto extremes; police service dysfunctional but courts function.

76434192B56312278962278.name: Western Cape
76434192B56312278962278.summary:
The Western Cape is the one province the dossier identifies as "usually scored as safest," with the strongest NGO infrastructure and the highest public visibility (Cape Town). No province-specific trans threat, ban, statute, enforcement action, or violent incident was found. For a foreign visitor, the practical implication is that the institutional response to a discovered trans person is a metro court, a PEPUDA-trained magistrate, and a visible civil-society network—the tier of protection that South Africa's constitutional enumeration of gender identity actually reaches in practice. The Hate Crime framework and the constitutional equality clause operate through functioning, accessible metro institutions here more than anywhere else in the country.

One unresolved sub-national question: Khoi-San communities in the Western Cape are pressing for recognition of indigenous authority structures unrecognised for three decades while Nguni chiefs are, with litigation over intangible cultural heritage (Khoin v Jenkins, 2022/2023). This is a parallel-authority recognition question in the safest province, not an existing jurisdiction that adjudicates gender or morality—no chief's court currently operates against a visitor in the Western Cape, and the litigation concerns cultural-heritage recognition, not criminal or moral adjudication of queer people. It is a small uncertainty against an otherwise clean provincial record.

The score is 0.03 above the national 0.69. vs. Gauteng (0.71), the Western Cape sits marginally higher because it has the highest public visibility and the strongest NGO infrastructure per capita, with a lower recorded-violence volume; both are metro-institution provinces but the Cape's NGO belt is more concentrated and accessible. vs. Limpopo (0.65) and North West (0.65), the gap of 0.07 reflects a fully functioning state-institution environment with active civil society against a rural customary-authority geography where the state's moral adjudication is mediated by a chief's court. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), the gap of 0.09 reflects the absence of a documented township queerphobia study and the absence of any royal or chiefly authority publicly aligning against queer people. vs. Northern Cape (0.64), the gap reflects a functioning institutional environment against a province that has produced a recorded trans murder.
76434192B56312278962278.modelContext: Cape Town: Africa's most open LGBT city — De Waterkant scene, Pride, tourism economy, and the Western Cape is the only province with consistently better-functioning provincial services; conservative religious communities in the Cape Flats/Boland coexist with the continent's most permissive urban envelope.

19338628B22645672383103.name: Île-de-France
19338628B22645672383103.summary:
Île-de-France sits fractionally below the national 0.67, but the deviation is small because the negative and positive factors largely cancel for a traveller. On the negative side, the Paris agglomeration and urban units over 200,000 inhabitants concentrate 55% of anti-LGBT offences for 43% of the population—a rate of 9 per 100,000, more than double the rural 4. The 2025 Marche des Fiertés was mobilised under a heavy police frame; the self-declared "gay patriot" collective Eros sought to march with prefectural backing, Inter-LGBT threatened to cancel if it participated, and participants reported that "the Marche des fiertés is becoming a sensitive event." A visitor attending the Pride encounters organisational tension and a security apparatus that signals vulnerability even as it protects.

On the positive side, the 9-per-100k rate is heavily inflated by reporting propensity, community visibility, dedicated police liaison desks and the density of associations—all of which mean more incidents are recorded and responded to, not necessarily that a visitor is at greater risk. Île-de-France has the country's densest trans support infrastructure and the largest community, giving a discovered visitor the best odds of institutional help and social buffer anywhere in metropolitan France.

Net deviation: −0.02 from national. The dossier's own caveat is explicit: "high recorded rates in Paris should not be read as Paris being dangerous." Compare with Bourgogne-Franche-Comté (0.62), where the state actively banned assembly; Île-de-France's state response to Pride was protective if tense. Compare with PACA (0.65), which shares the metro-rate exposure but adds the Fréjus dress-code incident as a specific negative on public appearance.
19338628B22645672383103.modelContext: Paris/Île-de-France: France's scene capital — Le Marais, national organizations (Inter-LGBT, OUTrans, Acceptess-T) all headquartered here, Pride draws hundreds of thousands; total anonymity; institutions fully protective.

19338628B95725112529620.name: Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur
19338628B95725112529620.summary:
PACA deviates −0.02 from the national 0.67. The region-specific negative is the RN mayor of Fréjus, David Rachline, issuing an arrêté on 1 August prohibiting swimming on communal beaches for anyone wearing "covering and loose clothing"—a dress-code order whose language directly reaches gender-nonconforming public appearance. However, the Toulon administrative tribunal suspended the arrêté and condemned the commune to €3,000 in August 2023, a clear institutional pushback. Per the enforcement-over-statute rule, a court-blocked municipal order carries small weight; its residual harm is the chilling signal it sends to a visitor who sees public dress policed by mayoral fiat, even if the specific order no longer operates.

PACA also shares Marseille's metro exposure: urban units over 200,000 record 9 per 100,000 anti-LGBT offences against the national ~5, a pattern driven by reporting density and visibility as much as by elevated actual incidence. The region's net position mirrors Île-de-France (0.65): a small negative from a specific municipal incident partially offset by a strong judicial correction, set against an urban-rate backdrop that the dossier explicitly cautions against reading as danger.

Compare with Hauts-de-France (0.64), where the RN pattern spans multiple communes and "around thirty associations" without a comparable single court suspension to offset it; PACA's one documented arrêté was fully and quickly reversed. Compare with Bourgogne-Franche-Comté (0.62), where the prefecture's ban was upheld rather than overturned—a materially different judicial outcome that justifies the two-unit spread between 0.62 and 0.65.
19338628B95725112529620.modelContext: Marseille/Nice/Cannes: Mediterranean tourism envelope — Riviera resorts historically permissive (Cassis/Cap d'Agde adjacent culture); Marseille working-class cosmopolitanism; FN/RN political strength in the hinterland is the counter-current.

28173009B98838729156012.name: Chechnya
28173009B98838729156012.summary:
Chechnya operates outside the Russian federal legal framework in practice. In February 2017, Chechen law-enforcement and security officials launched an anti-gay purge, rounding up dozens of men, holding them in unofficial detention facilities (documented by name and location, including a secret prison in Argun), humiliating, starving, and torturing them, forcibly disappearing some, and returning others to families "barely alive from beatings" after captors exposed them and encouraged relatives to carry out honour killings (HRW, 2017). Novaya Gazeta reported in January 2019 that persecution had resumed and the Argun facility was "full again," while Kadyrov's press chief publicly denied any unofficial detention sites exist.

The pattern has mutated and continues: North Caucasus SOS documented at least seven cases of Chechen security forces blackmailing detained homosexual men into "volunteering" for front-line conscription in Ukraine (one already killed), and Memorial found a mass wave of unlawful detentions tied to forced conscription. In 2021, Kadyrov's aide announced the abduction of two men evacuated abroad, taken at the Gudermes police station. The UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) explicitly names the North Caucasus as the exception to its finding of no state-persecution risk elsewhere in Russia.

For a visitor discovered or outed, the evidence indicates near-certain detention without legal process, torture, coerced conscription or death, with no functioning judicial remedy. This is approximately 0.11 below the national score of 0.12, reflecting a governance system where the state's security apparatus operates outside all legal constraint. Far below every other unit in the federation; even Dagestan and Ingushetia (0.04), which share the North Caucasus security logic, lack Chechnya's documented scale of extrajudicial killing and secret-prison infrastructure.
28173009B98838729156012.modelContext: Chechnya: purge-scale persecution since 2017 — abductions, secret prisons, torture killings, family-honor killings encouraged by authorities; being LGBT is treated as a capital offense in practice; the most dangerous jurisdiction in Europe/Central Asia for a trans person.

28173009B24428243574749.name: Dagestan
28173009B24428243574749.summary:
Dagestan falls within the North Caucasus regional exception identified by the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) and named in Canadian and Australian travel advisories as part of a distinct don't-travel zone. Canada specifically warns that visitors must obtain special permission from the Ministry of the Interior to enter certain areas. North Caucasus SOS's David Isteev states flatly that "there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families," adding that "every year it gets worse."

No separate Dagestan-specific written law or documented Chechnya-style purge exists, but the republic shares the same security-and-custom enforcement logic: the federal transition ban and propaganda law operate in a context where local security structures and family honour norms produce extrajudicial responses unmediated by legal process, and where special-access restrictions impede independent monitoring and foreign consular support. This places Dagestan approximately 0.08 below the national score of 0.12. Well below the oblasts of central Russia (which sit at national) due to the regional-exception designation; above Chechnya (0.01), whose documented secret-prison and killing infrastructure has no confirmed equivalent in Dagestan.
28173009B24428243574749.modelContext: Dagestan: Caucasus purge spillover — documented vigilante killings, police collusion with families, honor violence; Islamic-conservative governance strongest in Russia here.

28173009B75413689166101.name: Ingushetia
28173009B75413689166101.summary:
Ingushetia is one of the republics explicitly named in the Canadian travel advisory's special-permission requirement (alongside Chechnya and Dagestan) and falls within the North Caucasus zone that the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) identifies as the exception to its finding of no state-persecution risk in Russia generally. Isteev of North Caucasus SOS states there is "no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus," where private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families.

Like Dagestan, Ingushetia shares the security-and-custom enforcement logic without a documented Chechnya-scale purge infrastructure. The special-access regime limits independent monitoring and foreign consular intervention. Score approximately 0.08 below national (0.12). Equal to Dagestan in evidence quality; well above Chechnya (0.01), which has confirmed secret prisons and extrajudicial killings absent here.
28173009B75413689166101.modelContext: Ingushetia: same Caucasus pattern as Chechnya/Dagestan — clan-honor governance, effectively zero tolerance.

28173009B46612801043871.name: Kabardino-Balkaria
28173009B46612801043871.summary:
Kabardino-Balkaria is named within the broader North Caucasus risk zone identified by the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) and Western travel advisories. North Caucasus SOS's assessment that there is "no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus" encompasses this republic. The local security-and-custom enforcement logic—where family honour norms and informal security structures can produce violence, detention, or forced return to families—applies, even absent a specific documented purge infrastructure.

Unlike Chechnya, Dagestan, and Ingushetia, no separate special-permission entry requirement is specifically named for Kabardino-Balkaria in the Canadian advisory, and no Chechnya-scale extrajudicial detention site has been documented here. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.07 below. Slightly above Dagestan/Ingushetia (0.04) to reflect the absence of the explicit special-access regime; well below the central-Russian oblasts, which sit at national.
28173009B46612801043871.modelContext: Kabardino-Balkaria: North Caucasus religious-conservative enforcement climate; less purge-scale than Chechnya but street-level danger high.

28173009B95588705134862.name: Karachay-Cherkessia
28173009B95588705134862.summary:
Karachay-Cherkessia falls within the North Caucasus regional exception identified by the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) and named in Western don't-travel guidance for the Caucasus zone. The North Caucasus SOS assessment of no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region applies here. The security-and-custom enforcement logic—informal detention, family exposure, violence unmediated by legal process—is the operative risk for a discovered visitor.

No Chechnya-style documented purge infrastructure or specific special-permission entry regime is identified for Karachay-Cherkessia. Approximately 0.07 below the national score of 0.12. Equal to Kabardino-Balkaria and North Ossetia in the broader North Caucasus bloc; above Dagestan and Ingushetia (0.04), which carry the explicit special-access designation.
28173009B95588705134862.modelContext: Karachay-Cherkessia: North Caucasus conservative; low salience but dangerous if visible.

28173009B7235812138525.name: North Ossetia–Alania
28173009B7235812138525.summary:
North Ossetia–Alania is included in the North Caucasus zone that the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) singles out as the exception to its general finding of no state-persecution risk in Russia. Western travel advisories name the republic within the broader Caucasus don't-travel area. The enforcement logic is the same as neighbouring republics: family honour norms and informal security structures can produce violence, detention, or forced return without legal process.

No Chechnya-scale secret-prison infrastructure or explicit special-permission entry requirement is documented for North Ossetia specifically. Approximately 0.07 below national (0.12). Equal to Kabardino-Balkaria and Karachay-Cherkessia in the broader North Caucasus bloc. Well above the central-Russian oblasts, which inherit the national score with no sub-national deviation.
28173009B7235812138525.modelContext: North Ossetia: Caucasus conservative-Christian counterpart; traditional honor culture; Beslan-legacy securitization.

28173009B89423349656391.name: Stavropol Krai
28173009B89423349656391.summary:
Stavropol Krai is named in the Canadian travel advisory's special-permission requirement (alongside Chechnya, Dagestan, and Ingushetia) and is included in the North Caucasus zone identified by the UK Home Office CPIN as the exception to Russia's general risk picture. The dossier specifically identifies the south-eastern part bordering Chechnya as subject to the same security-and-custom enforcement logic. However, Stavropol is a krai, not a republic, and the extreme documented violence (secret prisons, purges, coerced conscription) is Chechen-specific rather than krai-wide.

For a visitor, the special-permission regime itself restricts movement and independent oversight, and the south-eastern areas adjacent to Chechnya share the localised security culture. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.05 below. Above the core North Caucasus republics (Dagestan, Ingushetia at 0.04; Kabardino-Balkaria, Karachay-Cherkessia, North Ossetia at 0.05) because the extreme evidence is geographically limited to the Chechnya border zone within a large multi-ethnic krai, and no independent republic-level security apparatus analogous to Kadyrov's exists.
28173009B89423349656391.modelContext: Stavropol: Caucasus gateway — Cossack patrol culture documented (moral-policing auxiliaries), conservative.

28173009B19676032168465.name: Moscow
28173009B19676032168465.summary:
Moscow concentrates enforcement activity of the federal anti-LGBT framework: club raids, the arrest of Kotov as the first person charged with *creating* an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds (late December 2024), and the medical and bureaucratic gatekeeping that the 2023 federal transition ban imposes. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution is titled around "arrests, club raids and extremism charges." A foreign visitor encountering Moscow police faces the federal propaganda-law penalty—up to 15 days' detention and deportation—applied in a jurisdiction with the highest police density and most active venue-level enforcement in the country.

The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.03 below. The severity of the law is identical everywhere (it is federal), but Moscow's role as the primary venue for enforcement operations and its concentration of bureaucratic touchpoints (document verification, medical access, hotel registration) materially raise a visitor's probability of encountering active application. Comparable to Orenburg Oblast (0.09), which produced the country's first criminal extremism conviction against a commercial venue; both represent enforcement-active jurisdictions within the uniform federal framework.
28173009B19676032168465.modelContext: Moscow: Russia's entire visible-underground scene — clubs operate discreetly, hormone access via private medicine, Pride banned since 2006 and attempts crushed, but the 12-million capital offers the only real anonymity; post-2023 'extremist movement' designation makes any organizing criminal everywhere including here.

28173009B76603557910928.name: Orenburg Oblast
28173009B76603557910928.summary:
Orenburg Oblast is the jurisdiction where the federal "LGBT extremism" designation first produced a criminal conviction against a commercial leisure venue. The Pose bar case (submitted to court July 2025 by the regional Investigative Committee) resulted in June 2026 in a seven-year sentence for owner Vyacheslav Khasanov, prison terms for two employees, and forfeiture of over one million rubles—Russia's first criminal LGBT-extremism sentencing. The precedent establishes that a bar or club can be prosecuted as an extremist organisation, which is the scenario a foreign visitor walking into a commercial venue is most likely to encounter.

This is visitor-facing enforcement: the venue context (drinking, socialising) is exactly where a visiting trans person might interact with the criminal justice system. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.03 below. Comparable to Moscow (0.09), which concentrates raids and the first organiser prosecution; both represent active enforcement venues within the uniform federal law. Orenburg's specific finding—a seven-year sentence against a bar owner—sets the most severe commercial-venue precedent in the country.
28173009B76603557910928.modelContext: Orenburg: Kazakh-border steppe; mixed conservative; Cossack presence.

36201628B69282955287113.name: NCR
36201628B69282955287113.summary:
NCR carries the strongest protective legal framework in the Philippines: Quezon City enacted SP-3417, S-2025, a comprehensive SOGIESC anti-discrimination ordinance, and in July 2025 became the first LGU in the country to enact a Gender-Inclusive Health Ordinance creating a framework for gender-affirming primary care and specialised services. For a visitor, these represent the only enforceable protections in a country with no national anti-discrimination statute covering gender identity—complaint routes to a city health office or the QC Gender Desk that simply do not exist elsewhere.

Against that, two of the six documented killings of trans women in the 2024–2025 national series occurred here (Shaina Bayabay strangled in Pasig, March 2024; "Christine" stabbed in Valenzuela, September 2025), and EARIST state college reportedly denied enrollment to trans women requiring short haircuts (March 2024 video). The Commission on Human Rights issued public statements condemning both the campus practice and the killings, and arrests followed in Valenzuela.

Net effect: +0.09 above the national score. The ordinance belt gives a discovered visitor tangible institutional recourse unavailable in sibling regions; the violence, while real, is matched by arrests and official condemnation rather than impunity. Compare Soccsksargen (0.44), where a targeted activist assassination drew the CHR's own "cruelty and impunity" language without comparable protective infrastructure.
36201628B69282955287113.modelContext: Metro Manila: the Philippines' scene capital — Malate/Poblacion visible gay bars, trans NGOs (STRAP, T-WANG) operate nationally from here, media visibility highest (Filipino entertainment's bakla/beauty-pageant culture gives public presence no ASEAN neighbor matches); city ordinances in Quezon City/Makati explicitly protect gender expression.

36201628B88329767373181.name: Central Visayas
36201628B88329767373181.summary:
Central Visayas holds the most active provincial-level anti-discrimination ordinance cluster outside Metro Manila. Mandaue City signed the Implementation Rules and Regulations of its Anti-Discrimination Ordinance in July 2024 in formal partnership with the KAABAG LGBT Federation and UNDP—an operational, not merely symbolic, protection framework. The municipality of Carmen, northern Cebu, approved a Comprehensive Anti-Discrimination Ordinance protecting people on SOGIE grounds by unanimous Sangguniang Bayan vote in June 2025.

No killings, assaults, or institutional hostility incidents specific to trans visitors or residents were documented in this region within the 2024–2025 violence series or elsewhere in the dossier.

Net effect: +0.07 above the national score. A visitor in Cebu/Mandaue can file an anti-discrimination complaint under an operational ordinance—the practical equivalent of the NCR protections without the accompanying violence signal. Compare Western Visayas (0.53), which shows the opposite pattern: institutional hostility (Capiz State University campus exclusion) without a compensating protective ordinance.
36201628B88329767373181.modelContext: Cebu: the Visayas' metro — Cebuano society is famously more relaxed on gender presentation than Manila (beauty-pageant/bakla culture deeply integrated); tourism economy; ordinances modest.

36201628B76469343449086.name: Soccsksargen
36201628B76469343449086.summary:
Soccsksargen is the site of the most severe single incident in the national trans-violence series: on 23 June 2025 in General Santos City, a hooded gunman shot Ali Jejhon Macalintal, a transgender rights activist and radio commentator, several times at the acupuncture clinic she owned, killing her; police explicitly investigated whether her history of activism was connected. Human Rights Watch called it an "apparent targeted killing." The Commission on Human Rights publicly condemned the killings as "marked by cruelty and impunity"—the strongest official language in the record, naming Macalintal specifically.

No protective ordinance, institutional counterweight, or positive enforcement response (arrest of the actual gunman) is documented. The "impunity" framing from the CHR is itself the damning signal the scoring rules identify as a large negative factor.

Net effect: −0.12 below the national score. This is the only unit where the violence is both targeted at trans-specificity and explicitly flagged as unaddressed by the official body. Compare NCR (0.65), which carries two killings but pairs them with arrests and the country's strongest protective ordinances; compare Calabarzon (0.51), where a single killing drew a homicide investigation within days.
36201628B76469343449086.modelContext: South-central Mindanao: most conservative Christian-settler region — General Santos traditional; adjacent Muslim-Mindanao culture; SOGIE-bill resistance strongest here; documented local hostility incidents.

36201628B47630810559445.name: Central Luzon
36201628B47630810559445.summary:
Angeles City and the Clark–Subic corridor in Pampanga constitute the region's principal traveler-facing risk. In June 2025 the NBI Bataan District Office dismantled a trafficking ring at Field Sensation's Bar in Angeles City, arresting four people and rescuing 45 victims including 13 minors; in March 2025 the same office arrested a foreign national and accomplices under the Expanded Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act, rescuing 12 more victims. Peer-reviewed research describes the US military-basing economy around Clark as sustaining sexual markets that "disproportionately exploit poor transgender Filipina women (trans-Pinays)," and the 2024 US TIP Report confirms traffickers exploit victims in tourist destinations and urban areas.

For a transgender visitor the exposure is two-fold: the environments where trans women are concentrated in sex work carry the highest violence and trafficking risk, and enforcement sweeps can sweep up anyone in the vicinity. There is no protective ordinance cluster here comparable to NCR or Central Visayas.

Net effect: −0.07 below the national score. The trafficking-exposure pattern is structural and documented rather than a single incident. Compare Calabarzon (0.51), which has one killing but no comparable commercial-sex-economy infrastructure drawing visitors into maximum-exposure environments.
36201628B47630810559445.modelContext: Pampanga/Bulacan: Angeles City's entertainment-bar economy creates documented trans visibility (and exploitation risk); Bulacan is church-conservative; mixed province-by-province.

36201628B13373758884154.name: Calabarzon
36201628B13373758884154.summary:
In August 2025 in Lipa City, Batangas, Jericho Elliorante, 25, newly crowned winner of an LGBTQ pageant in Barangay Sambat, Tanauan City, was found with 13 stab wounds. Police opened a homicide case within days of the crowning—a faster institutional response than the unresolved Macalintal shooting in Soccsksargen, but the incident still represents one of the six national killings and occurred in a region with no protective ordinance cluster.

Net effect: −0.05 below the national score. The single-incident rule applies: one killing in eighteen months is not a patterned violence trend for this unit, but the stabbing with 13 wounds and the LGBTQ-pageant context mark it as trans-implicated. The positive element (rapid homicide investigation) prevents a deeper deviation. Compare Cagayan Valley (0.52), whose single killing involved alleged kidnapping and rape—slightly more prolonged violence but also a three-suspect identification within weeks; Calabarzon edges below on the severity of the 13-wound attack.
36201628B13373758884154.modelContext: Southern Tagalog: Manila's commuter orbit — urban spill-over tolerance; provincial towns traditional-Catholic.

36201628B63748016552864.name: Cagayan Valley
36201628B63748016552864.summary:
On 31 July 2024 in Ilagan City, Isabela, Morine "G." Cabansag, 40, was found dead in a cemetery after an alleged kidnapping and rape in Centro San Antonio; three suspects were identified. This is one of the six killings in the 2024–2025 national series. No protective ordinance, institutional hostility finding, or enforcement pattern specific to trans visitors was documented in Cagayan Valley beyond this single incident.

Net effect: −0.04 below the national score. The kidnapping-plus-rape-plus-murder sequence is severe in manner, but the rapid identification of three suspects and the absence of any patterned regional signal (compared, for instance, to the commercial sex-economy structure in Central Luzon at 0.49) keep the deviation modest. Compare Soccsksargen (0.44), where the killing was a targeted assassination explicitly condemned by the CHR with the word "impunity" and no protective counterweight.
36201628B63748016552864.modelContext: Northern valley; traditional agricultural conservatism; Tuguegarao modest.

36201628B91065962446027.name: Western Visayas
36201628B91065962446027.summary:
In October 2022 the Capiz State University Office of Student Affairs informed students perceived as trans women that they would be barred from university premises unless they conformed on hair and clothing—a documented episode of institutional gender-expression policing in a provincial (not metropolitan) setting. The Alternative Law Groups case study records the subsequent advocacy campaign and a later milestone in reversing the exclusion.

No protective anti-discrimination ordinance comparable to those in Central Visayas or NCR is documented in this region. No killings from the 2024–2025 series occurred here.

Net effect: −0.03 below the national score. The campus exclusion is a climate signal rather than a traveler-facing criminal or facility-exposure risk, and the subsequent reversal by advocacy counts as a good institutional response under the single-incident rule. It sits slightly below national because the episode demonstrates that in a conservative provincial setting, expression can be policed by institutional authority without legal recourse, and the region lacks the protective-ordinance belt present in Central Visayas (0.63).
36201628B91065962446027.modelContext: Iloilo/Bacolod: gentler Visayan culture, strong university presence; Boracay (Aklan) tourism envelope with visible trans workforce in hospitality.

36201628B64564033926366.name: Ilocos Region
36201628B64564033926366.summary:
The Pangasinan provincial board certified and affirmed Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023 of Bayambang protecting the rights of LGBTQI persons (Provincial Board Resolution No. 799-2024, session of 19 August 2024)—a provincial-level endorsement of a municipal LGBTQ+ protection ordinance in a conservative province. This gives a visitor in the Pangasinan corridor a local complaint route absent in most other regions.

Against that, the Abra and Ilocos Sur provinces within Ilocos Region host the Bodong Indigenous Allied Group (BIAG), a codified customary-justice system with its own dispute-resolution authority over "crimes and tribal-related offences," recognised by Philippine courts. No trans-specific bodong ruling or customary exclusion was documented, but the legal-pluralism structure means that in a rural Abra or Ilocos Sur dispute, the applicable institution may not be a Philippine court.

Net effect: +0.03 above the national score, modest because the protective ordinance is municipal and the plural-justice uncertainty is localized to specific provinces within the region. Compare Central Visayas (0.63), where the ordinance cluster is broader (city IRRs with UNDP backing, unanimous municipal votes) and there is no countervailing alternative-justice structure.
36201628B64564033926366.modelContext: Ilocos: Marcos-heartland conservatism — traditional Ilocano society, strong church influence; Vigan tourism small-scale.

36201628B49646111072560.name: ARMM
36201628B49646111072560.summary:
ARMM (predecessor to BARMM) is the only unit where a structurally different legal system applies to a visitor in conflict situations. The Bangsamoro Administrative Code (BAA-13, 2019) provides that justice in the autonomous region shall be dispensed "in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws." Parliament Bill No. 473 (July 2026) proposes a comprehensive Bangsamoro Shari'ah Justice System Code adding ta'zir criminal offences—the category under which morality offences against same-sex conduct and gender expression are prosecuted in comparable systems. Nationally, the Shari'ah court system is expanding: President Marcos Jr. signed a law in August 2024 creating three new Shari'ah judicial districts beyond BARMM, RA 12304 (September 2025) ensures equitable access, and the Supreme Court resolved in January 2026 to operationalise the Shari'ah High Court.

The dossier's assessor caveat is explicit: no source establishes that Philippine Shari'ah courts currently prosecute same-sex conduct or gender expression, and the original P.D. 1083 codified only personal law. The finding is structural—a jurisdiction with an active legislative process to create criminal religious law, in a region where a visitor's dispute may be adjudicated outside the Philippine court system entirely—rather than a documented enforcement reality.

Net effect: −0.07 below the national score. The risk is forward-looking and legal-framework-based, not enforcement-based, which limits the deviation under the "enforcement > statute" rule. However, the ta'zir drafting is the single most severe structural threat identified in the dossier for a transgender visitor, and the absence of any protective ordinance or civil-rights infrastructure in ARMM means no counterweight exists. Compare CAR (0.54), which also has a legal-pluralism concern but no criminal-law component.
36201628B49646111072560.modelContext: Bangsamoro (Muslim Mindanao): sharia-influenced governance framework for Muslim residents under the BARMM organic law — gender expression socially invisible; for a visitor, Islamic-conservative social codes dominate; Cotabato City is the administrative center.

36201628B92932511992503.name: CAR
36201628B92932511992503.summary:
The Kalinga bodong/pagta system—bilateral inter-tribal peace pacts with their own holders, sanctions and dispute-resolution authority over "crimes and tribal-related offences"—was formally codified by the Kalinga provincial government in February 2026 as a 137-page written Pagta. Philippine courts recognise the bodong; academic literature frames it as legal pluralism in which indigenous and formal criminal justice coexist, with police handling customary-law cases. For a visitor whose dispute falls under a bodong's jurisdiction, the applicable institution may not be a Philippine court.

No trans-specific bodong ruling, customary exclusion, or gender-expression punishment was documented in the dossier. The constitutional recognition of indigenous justice also appears in the Bangsamoro Basic Law's IP-rights section, reinforcing the framework.

Net effect: −0.02 below the national score. The finding is a structural uncertainty (which court applies to you) without any evidence of trans-specific adverse outcome. It sits at the threshold of the minimum deviation. Compare ARMM (0.49), where the legal-pluralism concern is paired with an active criminal-law drafting process (ta'zir offences) that raises the stakes materially; here the bodong is a civil/ADR institution with no criminal-law expansion documented for morality offences.
36201628B92932511992503.modelContext: Cordillera highlands: indigenous Igorot societies — gender norms traditional but mountain-community smallness means low harassment salience; Baguio is the region's university city with a modest scene and cooler climate of tolerance.

68945753B94077674833362.name: Daegu
68945753B94077674833362.summary:
Daegu carries the most sustained municipal hostility to a public queer event in South Korea, justifying a −0.07 deviation below the national 0.71. City officials directly clashed with police as municipal workers attempted to prevent Daegu Queer Cultural Festival organisers from setting up at their Jung District venue; the PPP mayor is named as the driver of the obstruction. Police, however, intervened to stop the municipal workers—an institutional response that partly mitigates the threat.

The festival, the second-oldest in Korea (since June 2009), has run every year for 17 years 'without fail… as a form of resistance against hate and discriminatory politics,' including 2025 ('We Will Not Be E(r)ased') and 2026 ('事必Q정'). This persistence signals that municipal obstruction is real but does not prevent the event, and that the annual counter-mobilisation (≈3,500 believers from 1,600 churches via the Daegu Christian Council, along a 450 m stretch held simultaneously with the festival) creates a high-density confrontational environment for a visible trans visitor during festival season. Outside those specific dates, everyday street risk is comparatively low per the dossier.

Compared to Seoul (0.66): Daegu's hostility is narrower in geographic scale but more directly obstructive to a traveler attending a specific public event. Seoul's 1.1-million megarally is a broader climate signal; Daegu's pattern is a repeated, concentrated interference at one venue every year. Both cities share the PPP-mayor-and-Pride framing; Daegu edges lower because the obstruction targets the event itself rather than surrounding it.
68945753B94077674833362.modelContext: Daegu: Korea's most conservative major city — 2009 Pride attempt met with organized Christian mob blockade (documented), Daegu Queer Culture Festival 2023 clash with city government under Hong Joon-pyo; TBC/church political power strongest here; scene exists fully underground.

68945753B85435209225479.name: Daejeon
68945753B85435209225479.summary:
Daejeon presents mixed evidence yielding a −0.02 deviation from the national 0.71. In October 2021 the Daejeon District Court issued Korea's most important pro-trans ruling, ordering cancellation of the Army's forced discharge of transgender soldier Byun Hee-soo and holding that the military should have considered her a woman when assessing fitness for duty—a landmark institutional recognition. In June 2024, after the Ministry of National Defense reversed the Army's 'natural death' classification and recognised her 2021 death as service-related, Byun was buried at the National Cemetery in Daejeon. Approximately 60 activists gathered to protest the burial, a visible public rejection of state recognition of a trans person at the nation's memorial ground.

The court ruling is a positive institutional signal but is historical (2021) and addresses a specific administrative-military dispute rather than establishing general protections; a visitor encounters no ongoing Daejeon-specific legal advantage. The burial protest is traveler-facing (public hostility in an open space) but small in scale (60 people) and non-repeating—per the single-incident rule, it barely moves the score absent pattern. Net: the two findings largely cancel, leaving a small −0.02 below national for the residual negative event in public space. Compared to North Chungcheong (0.69), which shares the Byun case's origin but lacks the positive court ruling, Daejeon's mixed record yields the same deviation from a different direction.
68945753B85435209225479.modelContext: Daejeon: science-capital — KAIST student culture gives modest liberal pocket; city conservative overall.

68945753B59172752195743.name: North Chungcheong
68945753B59172752195743.summary:
North Chungcheong (capital: Cheongju) is scored −0.02 below the national 0.71 on the basis of the Byun Hee-soo case and its institutional aftermath, with the single-incident caveat applied explicitly. Byun, 23, was found dead in her Cheongju home on 3 March 2021 (apparent suicide) following forced military discharge and during ongoing mental-health counselling at a centre near her residence. Initial police and Army handling classified the death as 'natural'; this was overturned only three years later (April 2024) when the Ministry of National Defense's Central Military Casualty Review Board recognised it as service-related. The wrongful initial classification is the evidence: it reflects an institutional denial of the connection between anti-trans policy and a trans person's death, corrected only after sustained advocacy.

Per the single-incident rule, one death cannot establish a Cheongju pattern, and no repeat violence data exists for this unit. It is included at −0.02 rather than zero because Chungcheongbuk-do is small enough for one nationally prominent case to carry weight, and because the institutional response (wrongful classification sustained for three years before correction) is a state-implicated finding. Compared to Daejeon (0.69), which hosts the positive court ruling that corrected the same institution's error, North Chungcheong's share of the Byun story is purely negative—but the deviation is identical because the correction (Daejeon court, MND board) already mitigates the initial harm.
68945753B59172752195743.modelContext: Chungbuk: provincial middle; conservative; low salience.

68945753B70752081047384.name: South Chungcheong
68945753B70752081047384.summary:
South Chungcheong (Chungcheongnam-do) receives a −0.02 deviation below the national 0.71 based on one finding: the Chungcheongnam-do Office of Education filed a joint submission with the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education as 'stakeholders (enforcing authorities)' in the Supreme Court dispute over the bill to repeal the Student Human Rights Ordinances. This places a second provincial education office on the de-protection side of a pending constitutional-level case, confirming the repeal campaign is not confined to Seoul.

The evidence is primarily resident-facing (student non-discrimination rules), carrying small weight for a traveler under the scoring rules. It is included at −0.02 because it demonstrates active institutional alignment with the Seoul abolition drive at provincial level—a pattern that shapes the general climate a trans visitor encounters in interactions with public offices, though no traveler-facing enforcement action, arrest, or event obstruction is documented for this unit. Compared to Seoul (0.66), whose education office is the lead enforcer and whose mayor, police, and courts carry multiple traveler-facing findings, South Chungcheong's single filing is far weaker evidence of risk; the deviation is correspondingly smaller. No other province-specific incident or enforcement series was identified for this unit.
68945753B70752081047384.modelContext: Chungnam: provincial middle — 2020s human-rights-ordinance repeal battles documented here (conservative mobilization succeeded in gutting them); among the more hostile provincial climates.

68945753B43731078897969.name: Gyeonggi
68945753B43731078897969.summary:
Gyeonggi is scored +0.02 above the national 0.71 on the basis of its historical role as the origin of South Korea's student human-rights protections. The model ordinance covering discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity was 'first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province,' from which it spread to Seoul and other offices before the current 2024–26 repeal wave. Gyeonggi is the reference case for the protective side of the institutional fight now being contested at the Supreme Court.

The deviation is small and the evidence is resident-facing (school non-discrimination rules), carrying limited weight for a traveler per the scoring rules. No Gyeonggi-specific enforcement action, event, incident, or police practice favouring or disfavours a visible trans visitor. The +0.02 reflects the modest signal of an institutional culture that produced the country's first such protection, set against the fact that Gyeonggi's subsequent superintendent (Jo Hee-yeon) blocked Seoul's 2024 repeal—further evidence of protective posture at the provincial education level. Compared to Seoul (0.66), whose council has twice voted to delete the same ordinance, Gyeonggi's origin-and-defence record is the clearest positive sub-national signal in the dossier, though its traveler-facing impact remains minimal.
68945753B43731078897969.modelContext: Gyeonggi wraps Seoul — Suwon/Yongnan satellite cities share the metro's relative openness; provincial towns traditional.

47653553B66835736668351.summary:

47653553B97418467345315.summary:
The Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled the entire trial over the killing of a transgender woman, holding that Chile's "femicide" (femicidio) offence — the strongest gendered-violence protection in the penal code — covers only "a person biologically female" and therefore the conviction could not stand as framed. The annulment occurred in Tarapacá, where the Iquique court exercises jurisdiction. Tarapacá accounted for 1.56 % of the national anti-LGBTI case total in 2024, a small-share region in which a single structural finding dominates the per-capita signal.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.08 deviation. The legal framework is unchanged (Law 21.120 and the femicide article remain on the books nationally), but the regional judiciary's operative interpretation in this instance creates a concrete protection gap for a trans person who is assaulted in Tarapacá. Compared with La Araucanía (0.65), Tarapacá is 0.01 lower: Araucanía's −0.07 is trend-based (+150 % rise, low visibility), whereas Tarapacá carries a specific court ruling that names trans women as outside the femicide definition.

47653553B84299910343297.name: RegiÃ³n de La AraucanÃ­a
47653553B84299910343297.summary:
Movilh's XXIV annual report (March 2026) identifies La Araucanía as the region where reported homo/transphobic cases rose most sharply in 2025 — up approximately 150 % year-on-year — during a year when the national total hit a record 3,620 documented cases (+27.1 %). Movilh interprets the pattern as the decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ+ themes have less public debate, stating this "appears aimed at obstructing" equality work.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.07 deviation, trend-driven rather than incident-specific. There is no trans-specific Mapuche customary-law jurisdiction or documented state-implicated violence in the dossier; the indigenous-note is structural context within a region under prolonged security conflict. 47653553B86325292267162.summary:
In 2024 a trans woman, Kenia Chacón, was the victim of an attempted femicide (femicidio frustrado) in Punta Arenas. The tribunal imposed four years of internación parcial against the five years of internación total requested by the prosecution; the victim's mother publicly denounced devaluation of the attack on the basis of her daughter's gender identity. 47653553B1207481020383.summary:

Metropolitana is the region of best and worst in the country compressed into one administrative unit. The deviation reflects institutional posture rather than demonstrated violence.

10402087B20892132820961.summary:
Berlin remains the German jurisdiction with the deepest anti-discrimination apparatus, the largest visible queer community and the most institutionalised protection infrastructure. Ahead of the 2025 Christopher Street Day (hundreds of thousands expected), organisers explicitly urged participants to "be vigilant" amid a rise in attacks on LGBTQ+ events across Germany, as reported by The Guardian. The warning is event-specific; everyday institutional reception for a visitor in Berlin is the most hospitable in the country.

14339913B89763821047858.name: Wales
14339913B89763821047858.summary:
Wales's devolved administration publicly maintains an LGBTQ+ Action Plan with a standing update page issued after the For Women Scotland judgment (19 December 2025), and has enacted statutory school guidance ("Rights, Respect, Equality," consultation May 2025) obliging schools to challenge bullying and harassment on gender-reassignment grounds with recording and monitoring, alongside a dedicated national guidance for supporting trans children in development through 2025–26. For a visitor the practical risk of service refusal is unchanged — the code binds Welsh facilities as equally as English ones — but the visible institutional commitment (Action Plan maintained, school recording obligations, FOI-disclosed guidance work) shapes policing culture and public discourse. Score sits +0.03 above the national anchor: Wales is not materially safer on facilities, but it is the only devolved administration actively counter-signalling the national climate with published protection programmes. Above England, which has no equivalent positive devolved signal.

14339913B6930312138089.name: Northern Ireland
14339913B6930312138089.summary:
Northern Ireland carries three sub-national negatives absent elsewhere in the UK: Education Minister Paul Givan ordered the 2019 transgender-pupils guidance withdrawn from the Education Authority website after the FWS ruling, calling it "unlawful and flawed"; the Justice Minister's attempt to include transgender people as a protected group in hate-crime sentencing reform was stalled (reported DUP obstruction); and the Rainbow Project records a pattern of paramilitary-flavoured anti-LGB&T violence including a pipe bomb thrown through the home of a trans woman in Derry/Londonderry described by PSNI as a "sectarian hate crime," a 2019 Belfast city-centre assault hospitalising a gay man, and an average of ~290 anti-LGB&T incidents per year (2013–2017) with rising transgender-identity strand counts to September 2025.

Counter-balancing: PSNI/NISRA track a separate "transgender identity" category (unlike England and Wales), evidencing institutional recognition; the Health Minister publicly defended gender-identity service funding (£800k+ uplift) against DUP/TUV criticism, showing the executive is split rather than uniformly hostile. No criminal ban on expression or police-enforced facility prohibition exists — the risk mechanism mirrors the national EHRC code (service refusal by staff) plus street-level violence.

82085004B70364588595557.name: Northern Territory
82085004B70364588595557.summary:
The Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (No. 27 of 2025, assented 30 October 2025; Part 3 in force 27 July 2026) removed the civil provision making it unlawful to "offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate" a person in public on the basis of a protected attribute, including gender identity. The NT is the only Australian jurisdiction that has actively reversed anti-discrimination protection rather than extended it; the government framed the rollback as "restoring freedom of speech and religion." For a visitor, public verbal abuse or humiliation directed at gender expression is now deliberately outside NT law while other states have brought it inside.

Federal protections continue to apply uniformly: the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 covers gender identity in every state and territory, and NT hate-crime penalty enhancements for SO/GI-motivated offences (2022 amendment, effective 2023) remain in force. No criminal expression ban, no facility-access ban, and no conversion-practice-specific enforcement issue arises for a short-term visitor beyond the general federal framework.

Remote-area context amplifies practical risk: Alice Springs records approximately 2,600+ assaults per year against a population of ~25,000, and trans community infrastructure in the NT is thin. A single domestic killing of a Tiwi Sistergirl (Darwin, October 2024) is recorded for completeness but is one non-patterned incident and does not support a regional violence finding on its own.

Vs the national score of 0.86, the NT sits 0.09 below: the deliberate legislative removal of the "offend, insult, humiliate" protection is the strongest negative sub-national signal in Australia, even though it is a civil-law rollback rather than a criminal prohibition. Vs Victoria (0.88), where the 2025 Anti-Vilification Act created the country's first criminal offence for public incitement against a trans person, the NT moved in the opposite direction in the same year.

82085004B60194602145168.name: Victoria
82085004B60194602145168.summary:
The Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025 (No. 11 of 2025, passed April 2025) created both civil and criminal vilification offences and extended protection beyond race and religion to disability, gender identity, sex, sex characteristics, sexual orientation and personal association (Equal Opportunity Act 2010, new Part 6A, s.102B). Victoria is the only Australian jurisdiction where public incitement against a trans person is now a criminal charge, not merely a civil complaint. The Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities 2006 binds public authorities and provides an independent review mechanism absent in NSW, WA and SA.

A Victorian coronial inquest into the deaths of five young transgender women (Bridget Flack, Heather Pierard, Matt Byrne, Natalie Wilson and a fifth identified only as "AS") found Victoria Police failed the search for Flack. Coroner Ingrid Giles issued nine recommendations calling for an overhaul of missing-persons risk assessment for trans people. Advocates characterised the police handling as "a terrible miscarriage of justice." The finding documents a serious institutional failure, but the reform process and the 2025 legislation represent a corrective institutional response that counts as positive evidence under the single-incident and institutional-response rules.

Academic review confirms that Victorian LGBT prison protections are policy-based and not legally enforceable, a cross-jurisdictional weakness.

Vs the national score of 0.86, Victoria sits 0.02 above: the criminal vilification offence is the strongest new legal protection in the country and the Charter adds a structural review mechanism, but the coronial finding on police failure toward a specifically vulnerable sub-population (trans women in sex-work-adjacent contexts) and the thinness of prison policy prevent a larger positive deviation. Vs ACT (0.88), which also has a rights statute and self-ID custody but no equivalent criminal vilification offence and no comparable institutional-failure finding, the two units are at parity from different evidence.

82085004B21656044714531.name: New South Wales

The Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 (No. 19 of 2024, bipartisan, in force 4 April 2025) makes practices directed at changing or suppressing sexual orientation or gender identity criminal offences punishable by up to five years' imprisonment, including taking a person interstate or overseas for the purpose or engaging a provider outside NSW. A civil complaints scheme runs through Anti-Discrimination NSW. NSW also operates an explicit self-identification prison-placement policy, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

Against these strong legal protections, NSW carries a concentrated violence pattern. Kimberley McRae was killed in her Coogee apartment (January 2020); the accused admitted killing her after learning she was transgender and the case went to murder trial (NSW Supreme Court), a positive institutional response. Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old Filipina trans woman who had arrived in Australia approximately six weeks earlier, was strangled; her killer received only 22 months on a consensual-strangulation account that ABC reporting showed the court never heard contested. Two killings of trans women in the same state within roughly a year, with one adequate and one clearly inadequate sentencing outcome, is recorded as a pattern plus a contested institutional response, not as isolated incidents. WA's Equal Opportunity Act 1984 protects the attribute of "gender history," defined as a person who "identifies as a member of the opposite sex by living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex." Reform is underway: the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 received assent on 26 September 2024, removing medical and surgical prerequisites for registration of a sex or gender change, with substantive commencement by proclamation. This feeds back into the scope of "gender history" for complaints purposes but is not yet fully in force as of the scoring date.

15666254B53975248776023.name: Kelantan
15666254B53975248776023.summary:
Kelantan is the only sub-national unit in Malaysia—and in all of Southeast Asia—that has legislated the very state of gender transition as a criminal offence. Clause 17 of the Kelantan Syariah Bill passed 12–13 August 2026 makes it an offence for a Muslim to change their own gender, cause another person's gender to be changed, or induce someone to do so, punishable by a fine up to RM3,000, imprisonment up to two years, or both. The state had already brought its first prosecution of a trans woman under the predecessor 2019 Enactment via a Jaheaik operation at a gathering of transgender individuals, heard at the Kota Bharu Syariah Court. Critically, the Federal Court struck down 16 of 18 provisions of the 2019 Enactment in February 2024 as outside state power; the Kelantan assembly resolved to re-enact them anyway, and did so in August 2026. That sequence demonstrates deliberate institutional commitment, not a stray provision.

This deviates well below the national score because Kelantan adds a qualitative legal risk absent elsewhere: criminalisation of identity/existence itself, not merely public-order or cross-dressing offences. The two-year imprisonment penalty and the completed prosecution set a precedent that other states compare against. A foreign Muslim trans visitor is squarely within jurisdiction; a non-Muslim visitor is technically outside Syariah but still exposed to the climate this creates. Compare Terengganu (0.11), whose hostility is expressed through signboards and stated intent to "incite hatred" but which has no comparable criminal provision targeting gender transition per se.

15666254B71460903090065.summary:
In May 2025 the Kuala Terengganu authority installed warning signboards about homosexual practice at several strategic locations in the state, framing homosexuality as "dirty." When criticised, state exco member Datuk Wan Sukairi Wan Abdullah confirmed this was the deliberate aim: the signboards were meant "to instil hatred towards such acts among the community." Twelve civil-society organisations including Justice for Sisters demanded removal as a human-rights violation. Terengganu additionally maintains a Hudud & Qisas Enactment 2002 that is unenforceable due to the federal Act 355 penalty cap but which signals an aspirational legal ceiling, and amended its Takzir provisions from December 2022.

The exco statement removes any ambiguity about intent. It is not criminalisation (compare Kelantan at 0.08, where being trans is itself an offence), but the atmosphere is explicitly and officially manufactured to be hostile. Compare Johor (0.12), whose RM400,000 rehabilitation centre targets convicted individuals after the fact, whereas Terengganu's signboards broadcast a blanket message to all who enter the state.

The event organiser was separately probed for "encouraging vice," which rights groups condemned. The raid's design—targeting trans women specifically while ignoring the remaining attendees—demonstrates that the enforcement apparatus functions to isolate and process transgender people as a category.

This deviates below the national score because it evidences active, large-scale, category-targeted enforcement by a state religious department against trans people gathered privately. For a visitor present at or near such an event, the risk is immediate: detention, investigation, and prosecution under the 1988 Enactment. The Kedah raid is comparable in severity to Terengganu (0.11) in demonstrating state capacity and willingness to act against trans people en masse, though Kedah's incident is older (2020) and the enforcement is under an older statute.
