65028918B28366581005022.name: West Java
65028918B28366581005022.summary:
The most concentrated wave of mob violence against transgender women in Indonesia: ten attacks on 45 victim-survivors in Bogor between 30 March and 15 July 2026. Attackers punched, kicked, threw stones, glass bottles and firecrackers, and stripped some victims naked. Groups of 10–20 men filmed the assaults for social media under the account @bogorbersihlgbt ("Bogor clean of LGBT"). No alleged perpetrator has been publicly identified, arrested, or prosecuted; a trans-rights activist accompanying women who filed police reports said officers "accepted the case but worked on it half-heartedly." Additionally, 75 people were detained at a Puncak-area villa raid (June 2025) violating no law. Activists attribute the violence to Perpres 111/2025 classifying "LGBT culture" as a non-military threat, stating "people feel able to commit violence arbitrarily because they believe the state has legitimised that violence."

This is well below the national score. Unlike Jakarta (0.12), where a discriminatory 56-man raid prompted immediate Amnesty demands and the detainees lacked legal charges, the Bogor wave shows patterned vigilante violence with total state inaction and explicit anti-trans branding over four months.
65028918B28366581005022.modelContext: Bandung/Bogor/Depok: the most populous province surrounds Jakarta with the strongest Islamist-organizational presence (Garut, Depok ordinances documented); vigilante pressure historically highest here; but Bandung's university scene exists.

65028918B4119458748300.name: West Sumatra
65028918B4119458748300.summary:
The clearest enacted modern local anti-LGBT bylaw outside Aceh: Bukittinggi City Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024, articles 43–44, prescribes oral and written warnings, cessation of activities, social rehabilitation programmes, and administrative fines of Rp1,000,000 targeting LGBT people. Limapuluh Kota regency finalised a draft ranperda on public tranquility containing an explicit LGBT prohibition with administrative fines and "rehabilitation" for people of same-sex attraction. Academic analysis notes implementation remains weak precisely because rehabilitation facilities do not exist. West Sumatra also appears in OutRight's eight-province discriminatory-regulation analysis.

This sits below the national score because an enacted bylaw with specified sanctions creates visitor-facing risk (detention, forced rehabilitation programmes, fines) that does not exist in most provinces. However, the documented absence of enforcement infrastructure and no recorded arrest or caning keep it above West Java (0.06), where patterned mob violence with zero accountability is the primary threat, and above the national floor where no such bylaw exists at all.
65028918B4119458748300.modelContext: Padang: Minangkabau matrilineal society is strongly Islamic-conservative in public morality despite matriliny; documented raids; Pariaman anti-LGBT bylaw precedent.

65028918B6690755070061.name: Bali
65028918B6690755070061.summary:
Bali offers the closest approximation to pockets of refuge in Indonesia: LGBTIQ+ people migrate there to "remake the meaning of home" and find spaces where they feel "valued, accepted and able to be themselves, even if those spaces are hidden and limited." No local enforcement actions, discriminatory bylaws, mass raids, or violence waves have been documented against trans visitors. The island sits outside OutRight's eight-province discriminatory-regulation set. However, the 2026 KUHP applies equally: Art. 412 criminalises sex outside marriage and cohabitation (up to one year, complaint-based by spouse/parent/child), and broad "indecency" provisions remain; travel guides discourage public displays of affection. A 2025 ethnographic study of transpuan communities in Bali explicitly challenges the "romanticised refuge" framing, documenting "resistance and misrecognition" and systemic discrimination even there.

The deviation above the national score reflects absent local enforcement rather than a legal exemption. Materially safer than Jakarta (0.12) with its hotel raids and discriminatory regs, but not a protected space; the new KUHP and Perpres 111/2025 create fresh exposure that could be activated in any police contact.
65028918B6690755070061.modelContext: Bali: Hindu-majority island where national Islamic-conservative pressure applies weakest; international tourism creates a real envelope; Seminyak scene visible; Indonesian police generally restrained on-island due to tourism economics.

65028918B16658067687714.name: Papua
65028918B16658067687714.summary:
No trans-specific incident series was found for Papua, but the dossier documents 138 recorded acts of torture or other ill-treatment in detention committed by police and military in Maybrat and the Central Highlands between September 2021 and Q1 2025, "with almost no consequences." Named arbitrary-detention cases include three Papuans detained by officers at Nop Goliat Airport, Dekai (Yahukimo) on 26 July 2025 while one was boarding to study in Jayapura. Q3 2025 saw expanded military deployments and forced displacement. For any visitor, including a transgender one, the probability that police contact escalates into unlawful detention and ill-treatment is documented and far above the national average. This is an amplifier finding on non-trans-specific evidence, not an independent conclusion about trans people.

It sits at the same level as West Sumatra (0.11) in deviation from the national score, though the mechanism differs: West Sumatra has an enacted bylaw with specified administrative penalties; Papua has a documented torture-and-arrest pattern that raises the severity of any encounter with security forces, without a trans-specific legal basis being needed.
65028918B16658067687714.modelContext: Papua: militarized conflict province; Indonesian security-force presence dominates; Papuan society traditionally gender-conservative; LGBT issues subsumed under security politics.

65028918B17554737605304.name: South Sulawesi
65028918B17554737605304.summary:
Makassar's mayor Munafri 'Appi' Arifuddin reaffirmed his commitment to pushing through an anti-LGBT Perda after a same-sex act at a night entertainment venue went viral; the deputy chair of the DPRD's legislation body backed it as "urgently needed to preserve moral order and religious norms." South Sulawesi is one of eight provinces in OutRight International's discriminatory-regulation analysis. No enacted bylaw with specified penalties yet exists, and no violence wave or mass police raid is documented in this province.

The small negative deviation from the national score reflects an active legislative push in a major domestic-tourism gateway to eastern Indonesia, raising the probability of future discriminatory enforcement. It remains above West Sumatra (0.11), where a Perda with articles 43–44 specifying fines and rehabilitation is already on the books, and above Jakarta (0.12), where a 56-person raid without legal basis has already occurred. The deviation is at the threshold because the law is proposed, not enacted, and per the enforcement-over-statute rule the traveler-facing impact is prospective.
65028918B17554737605304.modelContext: Makassar: 2023 documented raid wave and anti-LGBT mobilization; but Bugis culture historically recognizes five genders (calabai/bissu traditions) — the deepest traditional gender-variant culture in Indonesia coexists with modern Islamist hostility.

65028918B9551391119865.name: South Sumatra
65028918B9551391119865.summary:
On 19 July 2026 the Palembang city government announced it was preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT, presented as follow-through on Presidential Regulation No. 111 of 2025, which lists the "spread of LGBTQ culture" among non-military threats to national defence alongside terrorism and trafficking. Mayor Ratu Dewa made the announcement in the courtyard of the Grand Mosque. South Sumatra also appears in OutRight's eight-province discriminatory-regulation set. The regulation remains in preparation, not yet enacted, with no specified penalty or enforcement event documented.

The deviation from the national score is small and below it, similar to South Sulawesi (0.13). The Perpres 111/2025 framing elevates local anti-LGBT rules from moral panic to national-defence doctrine—activists say this legitimised the Bogor mob violence—but without a specific enacted penalty the traveler-facing risk remains prospective. It sits above West Sumatra (0.11), which has a live bylaw with specified sanctions in articles 43–44, and above the national floor where no equivalent regulation has been announced.

1875124B91024374055933.name: La Libertad
1875124B91024374055933.summary:
The Public Ministry's 2012–2021 study places La Libertad second in absolute LGTB-homicide count (10 of 88), centred on Trujillo. The region's population share (~3%) is far smaller than its death share (~11.4%), giving a per-capita lethality roughly 3.8× the national average—a materially concerning concentration that is not explained by population alone and places the unit below the national 0.36.

Counterweight: Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR (published in El Peruano, November 2024) promotes labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender people. This is a resident-facing instrument (a visitor does not use it) and carries only small weight under the scoring rules, but it evidences that this particular regional council legislated visibly for trans inclusion—the one such ordinance found in Peru's 26 departments. It also sits in the same department where rondas campesinas exercise recognised dispute-resolution authority, a structural caveat with no documented trans-specific case.

Net deviation: −0.02 from national. The per-capita violence concentration is the dominant factor; the ordinance prevents a larger deduction. vs Lima (0.33): La Libertad's per-capita rate is worse, but Lima's higher absolute count, 2025 case, and crime-reporting concentration keep it slightly below. vs Tacna (0.34): both are modestly below national, but La Libertad's multi-year dataset is more robust evidence than a single incident.
1875124B91024374055933.modelContext: Trujillo: northern conservative coastal city; modest scene; crime rates elevated.

1875124B58976419670313.name: Tacna
1875124B58976419670313.summary:
On 19 April 2025, Marcia Paucara Cora (48), a trans woman, was found dead by mechanical asphyxia in a hospedaje room in Tacna; the man seen entering with her fled and remains unidentified. The case is being investigated as a possible hate crime (reported by Wayka and Trome). This is the first documented such killing in this small border department. Under the single-incident rule, a lone killing moves a score only slightly unless patterned or state-implicated; here the perpetrator is unidentified and the state's response is active (hate-crime framing) though there is no hate-crime statute to charge under nationally.

Deviation: −0.02 from national 0.36. The justification is the per-capita impact in a small population (Tacna department ~300,000) where one killing is statistically notable, combined with the absence of a hate-crime enhancement meaning the legal response is identical to ordinary homicide. No facility ban, expression criminalisation, or police-targeting evidence specific to Tacna was found. The investigation-as-hate-crime posture is a marginally positive institutional signal.

vs Lima (0.33): Lima's multi-year concentration and 2025 case provide a thicker evidence base for a larger deduction. vs La Libertad (0.34): both are −0.02; La Libertad's 10-death dataset is far more robust but is partially offset by its protective ordinance, while Tacna's single case has no counterweight, netting them level.

13589884B77991835419453.name: Atlántico
13589884B77991835419453.summary:
Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report issues a specific, named warning of "increasing violence against LGBTIQ+ people in the Atlántico department," situating Barranquilla within the national territorial-expansion finding rather than treating it as an undifferentiated count. Barranquilla is the Caribbean-coast hub for trans sex work and the city where the NGO's documentation base operates, giving it both elevated exposure and visibility in monitoring data. The department appears explicitly in the 270-victim national total.

Versus the national score (~0.52), Atlántico falls approximately 0.09 lower, justified by the NGO's named escalation warning (not merely inclusion in aggregate counts, but a specific "increase" call-out) and the structural role of Barranquilla's trans sex-work corridor. Versus Antioquia (0.33), Atlántico is higher: its violence is a rising trend flagged by Caribe Afirmativo rather than the decade-deep, impunity-saturated lethality concentration that makes Antioquia "one of the most dangerous" in Colombia. Versus Bolívar (0.44), Atlántico sits marginally lower because its finding is a forward-looking escalation warning tied to a specific urban hub, whereas Bolívar's deviation rests on one targeted killing of a named community leader.
13589884B77991835419453.modelContext: Barranquilla: Carnival culture has documented gender-transgressive traditions (marimondas, transformismo); city violence is cartel-general.

13589884B96168520946689.name: Bolívar

El Tiempo's data-journalism work on the gap between official Fiscalía and NGO (Caribe Afirmativo/Defensoría) figures names her case specifically. Bolívar appears within the Caribbean-coast cluster flagged by Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 territorial-expansion finding, where state response is weakest.

Versus the national score (~0.52), Bolívar sits approximately 0.08 lower: the killing is a named, targeted murder of a community leader (not an undifferentiated count), and the department falls within the "territorial expansion" zone where the monitoring body documents insufficient state protection. Versus Antioquia (0.33), Bolívar is substantially higher because it carries one specific high-profile homicide rather than the 45-of-270 structural concentration and multi-case impunity pattern defining Antioquia. Versus Atlántico (0.43), Bolívar is marginally above: its evidence is a single named killing within an aggregate warning, whereas Atlántico carries a forward-looking escalation call-out tied to a larger trans sex-work hub.
